cards.title: Temporal vs Queues
cards.question: Why move 9 integrations onto a workflow engine like Temporal instead of chaining jobs on a queue?
points: Durable execution: state is saved as an event history, so a workflow resumes exactly where it stopped after a crash
Retries, timeouts and backoff are declared per activity, not hand-written for each integration
Long waits (hours or days) are built in, so no polling jobs or cron glue
Every run has an inspectable history, which makes debugging and on-call much easier
Cost: a new mental model, and workflow code must be deterministic
cards.weakness: What were the hardest parts of adopting Temporal?

points: A new mental model: workflows replay, so code must be deterministic
Versioning workflows while old runs are still going
Running the Temporal cluster, or paying for Temporal Cloud
Teaching the team to test and debug it; have your own examples ready

cards.title: The Temporal Migration
cards.question: Tell me about leading Fynd's first Temporal rollout: 9 integrations and about 80 workflow stages in 9 to 12 months.
points: Situation: each marketplace integration had grown its own special cases over years
Task: you led the company's first Temporal adoption and owned the shared workflow model
Action: be ready to explain the shared model and how you moved integrations over one at a time
Result: 9 integrations and ~80 stages on one model, replacing per-integration special cases
Close with one lesson and what you would do differently
cards.weakness: How did you migrate live sellers without breaking their order flow?

points: Common approaches: migrate one integration, or one group of sellers, at a time
Run old and new side by side and compare results before switching
A per-seller flag to switch back instantly
Be ready to say exactly what you did and what went wrong

cards.title: Determinism
cards.question: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?
points: After a crash, a worker rebuilds workflow state by replaying the event history
Replay must issue the same commands in the same order, or Temporal flags a non-determinism error
So no Date.now(), Math.random() or direct I/O inside workflows
Side effects go in activities; use the workflow APIs for time and sleep
Changing running workflows needs versioning (patching)
cards.weakness: How do you change workflow code while old runs are still in flight?

points: Use versioning: patched() branches between old and new code
Running workflows replay the old path; new ones take the new path
Remove the old branch once no old runs remain
Worker versioning (build ids) pins runs to the code that started them

cards.title: Workflows & Activities
cards.question: In Temporal, what is the difference between a workflow and an activity?
points: Workflow: the orchestration logic. Deterministic and durable
Activity: the real work with side effects (API calls, DB writes). Allowed to fail
Activities are retried by a retry policy with backoff
Timeouts: start-to-close, schedule-to-close, heartbeat
Workers poll task queues to run both
cards.weakness: What is an activity heartbeat for?

points: Long-running activities report 'still alive' regularly
If heartbeats stop, Temporal times the activity out quickly instead of waiting the full timeout
Heartbeats can carry progress, so a retry resumes where it stopped
Cancellation is delivered to the activity through heartbeating

cards.title: Per-Seller Rate Limits
cards.question: How do you respect Amazon, Flipkart and Shopify rate limits while syncing catalogues of up to 300,000 SKUs?
points: Limits apply per seller credential, so throttle per seller, not globally
Queue the work and let workers pull only at the allowed rate (token bucket)
On 429, honour Retry-After and back off exponentially with jitter
Batch updates into feeds instead of one call per SKU
Only sync what changed since the last run
cards.weakness: What is jitter, and why add it to backoff?

points: Jitter adds randomness to each retry delay
Without it, every client that failed together retries together
Those synchronized waves keep overloading the service
Full jitter: wait a random time between 0 and the backoff
ex.answer:
const delay = Math.random() *
  Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)

cards.title: Silent Schema Change
cards.question: A marketplace quietly changes its API response format. How do you find out before your sellers do?
points: Validate responses at the boundary against a schema and fail loudly
Contract tests against the OpenAPI spec (Specmatic) catch drift in CI
Alert on spikes in parse or validation errors per marketplace
Tolerate unknown extra fields, fail on missing required ones
Pin API versions where the marketplace supports it
cards.weakness: Strict or tolerant parsing: which do you pick and why?

points: Tolerant of extra fields: new optional data should not break you
Strict on fields you depend on: missing or wrong type fails loudly
Silent defaults turn API changes into wrong data downstream
Log and alert on failures so you notice in minutes

cards.title: Multi-Market Sync
cards.question: Design inventory and order sync for a seller with 300,000 SKUs across Amazon, Flipkart and Shopify.
points: Postgres is the source of truth; track changes so you only push deltas
One adapter per marketplace behind a shared interface
A queue per seller and marketplace that respects rate limits and batches feeds
Idempotent upserts on external IDs, retries with backoff, dead-letter queue
A reconciliation job compares counts to catch drift; metrics per seller
cards.weakness: Two marketplaces sell the last unit at the same moment. What happens?

points: Both accept the order, so you are oversold by one
Reserve stock atomically in your own database as orders arrive
Keep a small safety buffer on each marketplace
Push stock changes fast; have a cancellation and seller-notification path

cards.title: Amazon VDF in 3 Months
cards.question: You delivered the company's first Amazon VDF integration in 3 months. Walk me through it.
points: VDF = Vendor Direct Fulfillment: the vendor ships Amazon orders straight to customers
Started from a design document: scope, order and shipment flows, risks
Explain how the shared workflow model sped things up
Milestones that kept it on track from design to production
Result: first VDF integration live in 3 months
cards.weakness: What was the riskiest part, and how did you de-risk it?

points: Name the biggest unknown: an unfamiliar API, a format, an external deadline
De-risk it early: a spike, sandbox calls, a thin end-to-end slice first
Show how you reduced scope or got help when needed
Have your real answer ready: this is about your story

cards.title: 70k Orders a Day
cards.question: Explain your BullMQ and Kafka pipeline: 70,000+ orders and feed updates a day within Amazon's feed limits, without delaying new orders.
points: Kafka carries the durable, replayable stream of order and inventory events
Consumers turn events into BullMQ jobs, which handle retries and rate limiting
Priorities: new orders jump ahead of bulk feed updates
Many updates are batched into one feed submission to stay under limits
70k a day averages ~0.8 per second, but peaks are bursty, so you buffer
cards.weakness: How do you keep new orders flowing when bulk feed updates spike?

points: Separate queues, or priorities, so new orders never wait behind feeds
Reserve part of the rate-limit budget for orders
Batch feed updates and let them lag when busy
Watch queue age per type and alert when orders slow

cards.title: Kafka vs BullMQ
cards.question: Kafka and BullMQ both move messages. What is each one good at?
points: Kafka: a partitioned log. Many consumer groups, replay, ordering per partition, huge throughput
Kafka has no per-message retry, delay or priority built in
BullMQ: a job queue on Redis with per-job retries, delays, priorities and a rate limiter
Use Kafka to fan events out between services
Use BullMQ to execute tasks with throttling and retries
cards.weakness: How does Kafka guarantee ordering?

points: Order is guaranteed only within one partition
Messages with the same key always go to the same partition
Each partition is read by one consumer in a group, in order
The idempotent producer keeps order even when it retries

cards.title: 0% to 70% Coverage
cards.question: You introduced the team's first automated tests for 9 integrations that had 0% coverage. How?
points: Situation: no tests, so third-party changes caused regressions
Jest and Mocha unit tests for mapping and business logic
Specmatic contract tests generated from the OpenAPI specs
A 70% coverage gate in Azure DevOps CI so it stayed enforced
How you got buy-in and chose what to test first (riskiest code)
cards.weakness: Is 70% a good coverage target? What does coverage not tell you?

points: It is a reasonable floor, not a goal
Coverage shows code ran, not that the right things were checked
Coverage on risky code matters more than the total
Pair it with contract tests and mutation testing for quality

cards.title: SSO & Seller Auth
cards.question: You set up Google SSO and per-seller IAM authentication for Amazon's APIs across 100+ sellers. Explain both.
points: Google SSO: OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0; Google returns an ID token
Each seller authorises the app, which stores credentials per seller
Short-lived access tokens are refreshed from stored refresh tokens
Credentials are encrypted and strictly scoped to one seller
Least-privilege IAM roles for API access
cards.weakness: Where did you store per-seller secrets, and how were they rotated?

points: Typical answer: in a secret manager or encrypted at rest, never in code
Access restricted to the services that need them, with audit logs
Refresh tokens renew access tokens automatically
Rotation and revocation when a seller disconnects; have your real setup ready

cards.title: On-Call Incident
cards.question: Tell me about a production incident you handled on-call.
points: Pick your best one of the 30+ and practise it until it is crisp
How it was detected and who was affected
Mitigate first: how you stopped the bleeding
Root cause, and how you talked to the client throughout
The RCA you wrote and what changed afterwards
cards.weakness: How do you talk to an upset client during an outage?

points: Acknowledge fast and say what you know, even if it is little
Give an expected time for the next update, and keep it
Stick to facts and impact; no blame and no guessing
Follow up with the root cause and what will prevent it

cards.title: Root Cause Analysis
cards.question: What goes into a good root cause analysis (postmortem)?
points: Timeline of what happened and when
Impact: who was affected and for how long
Root cause, found by asking why repeatedly (5 whys)
Action items with owners and dates
Blameless: focus on systems, not people
cards.weakness: Why should postmortems be blameless?

points: People hide mistakes when they fear blame, so you lose the real story
Most incidents come from systems that made a mistake easy
Fixing the system prevents repeats; blaming a person does not
Accountability stays: owners commit to action items

cards.title: No-Code Builder
cards.question: You built a no-code workflow builder used daily by 5+ product managers. Tell me about it.
points: Problem: every new integration needed engineering time
Built with React, TypeScript and React Flow
Iterated with the PMs who used it every day
Result: new integrations needed 50% less engineering help
Be ready to say how the 50% was measured
cards.weakness: How do you stop a PM from saving a workflow that cannot run?

points: Validate the graph on save: one trigger, connected nodes, required fields filled
Show errors on the exact node, in plain language
A test run with sample data before publishing
Versions: a broken edit never replaces the live workflow

cards.title: Workflow Platform
cards.question: Walk me through your Workflow Automation Platform.
points: No-code: users chain API calls on a drag-and-drop React Flow canvas
4 node types: triggers, conditions, loops and actions
The graph is saved as JSON and executed on Temporal
Retries and step-by-step tracing for every run
100/100 runs of a 20-step workflow passed against an API failing 30% of calls
cards.weakness: How do you turn a graph on a canvas into something executable?

points: Save nodes and edges as JSON, with a version
Validate the graph before running it
An interpreter walks it from the trigger, following edges
Each node runs as a Temporal activity, so every step is retried and traced

cards.title: Running the Graph
cards.question: How do you safely execute a user-drawn graph with conditions and loops?
points: Validate first: one trigger, no dangling edges, cycles only through loop nodes
Walk from the trigger, following edges
Condition nodes choose which outgoing edge to follow
Loop nodes get a max-iteration guard so nothing runs forever
Each action is a Temporal activity with its own retry policy; record inputs and outputs per step
cards.weakness: How would you add parallel branches?

points: Add a fork node that starts several branches at once
In the workflow, run the branch activities concurrently and await them all
A join node waits for all (or the first) and merges their outputs
Decide what one failing branch does: fail the run or continue

cards.title: 100 out of 100
cards.question: How did you prove the platform survives failures?
points: A mock API failed 30% of calls at random
Ran a 20-step workflow 100 times; all 100 completed
Without retries, all 20 steps succeeding is 0.7^20, about 0.08%
Retries with backoff on every step made the difference
Killed the server mid-run; Temporal resumed from the event history
cards.weakness: What would break if the mock API calls were not idempotent?

points: Retries would repeat side effects: double charges, duplicate records
The 100/100 result would hide data corruption
Real APIs need idempotency keys, or a check before retrying
That is why idempotency matters as much as retries

cards.title: React Flow
cards.question: What is React Flow, and how do custom nodes work?
points: A library for node-based UIs: nodes, edges and handles
State is arrays of nodes and edges, updated via onNodesChange and onEdgesChange
Custom nodes are React components registered in a nodeTypes map
Handles are the connection points on a node
isValidConnection can block invalid links
cards.weakness: How do you keep a large canvas fast?

points: Memoize custom node components with React.memo
Keep node data stable: no new objects or functions each render
Read state with selectors so one change does not re-render everything
onlyRenderVisibleElements skips off-screen nodes

cards.title: Four Node Types
cards.question: Why triggers, conditions, loops and actions? Why those four?
points: Trigger: starts a run (webhook, schedule or manual)
Action: does the work, usually an API call
Condition: branches the flow
Loop: repeats over a list
Together they cover sequence, branching and iteration
cards.weakness: What node type would you add next, and why?

points: A Delay node: wait minutes or days, cheap with Temporal timers
A Parallel node: run branches at the same time
A Transform node: reshape data between steps
An Error handler: catch failures and branch, instead of failing the run

cards.title: Zero Lost Events
cards.question: Walk me through how FormHook makes sure no webhook event is lost when an endpoint fails.
points: Each event is saved as a BullMQ job in Redis before any delivery is attempted
Up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff, giving a flaky endpoint time to recover
After the last failure the job moves to a dead-letter queue to inspect and replay
A failure-simulation mode injects errors and timeouts to prove recovery works
Runs on EC2, provisioned with Terraform for one-command setup and teardown
cards.weakness: Why save the event before trying to deliver it?

points: If the server crashes between receiving and sending, the event is gone
Saving first makes it durable before you acknowledge it
You can answer the sender quickly (202 Accepted) and deliver later
Delivery speed and failures no longer affect intake

cards.title: Duplicate Delivery
cards.question: The endpoint received your webhook but timed out before replying, so you retry. How do you stop it being processed twice?
points: Exactly-once delivery over a network is not possible; aim for at-least-once
Send a unique event ID (idempotency key) with every delivery
The receiver stores seen IDs and ignores repeats
Retries reuse the same ID
Document this so receivers know to dedupe
cards.weakness: How long should a receiver remember event IDs?

points: At least as long as the sender may still retry
Plus the window in which you might replay from the dead-letter queue
Often 24 to 72 hours, stored with a TTL
Too short lets late duplicates through; too long costs storage

cards.title: Exponential Backoff
cards.question: Why use exponential backoff instead of retrying straight away?
points: Gives a failing service time to recover
Avoids a retry storm hammering a struggling endpoint
Delays grow: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
Add jitter so clients do not all retry at the same instant
Cap the max delay and the number of attempts
cards.weakness: What is the thundering herd problem?

points: Many clients wake up or retry at the same moment
They all hit one service at once and overwhelm it
It recovers, they retry together again, and it falls over again
Jitter and staggered start times spread them out

cards.title: Dead-Letter Queue
cards.question: What is a dead-letter queue, and why have one?
points: Holds messages that failed every retry
Stops a poison message from blocking the queue
Keeps the data so nothing is silently lost
Inspect, fix, then replay
Alert when it starts filling up
cards.weakness: What is a poison message?

points: A message that fails every time it is processed
Bad data, an unexpected format, or a bug triggered by its contents
Retrying forever blocks the queue and wastes resources
Move it aside after a few attempts and alert

cards.title: Failure Simulation
cards.question: Why build a failure-simulation mode into FormHook itself?
points: Chaos engineering on a small scale: break things on purpose
Proves retries and the dead-letter queue actually work
Makes timeouts and errors reproducible in tests
Cheaper than waiting for a real outage to find bugs
Must be impossible to switch on by accident in production
cards.weakness: How do you make sure failure simulation can never run in production?

points: Off by default; switched on only by an explicit setting
The service refuses to start with it on in production
Inject failures only in non-production builds or behind an admin-only flag
Log loudly whenever it is active

cards.title: Signed Webhooks
cards.question: How does a webhook receiver know a request really came from you?
points: Sign the body with HMAC using a shared secret and send it in a header
The receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares
Use a constant-time comparison
Include a timestamp and reject old requests to stop replays
Always over HTTPS
cards.weakness: Why does the comparison need to be constant-time?

points: A normal comparison stops at the first different character
An attacker can time responses to guess the signature byte by byte
Constant-time comparison always takes the same time
Node: crypto.timingSafeEqual
ex.answer:
crypto.timingSafeEqual(
  Buffer.from(expected),
  Buffer.from(received),
)

cards.title: Leitner System
cards.question: How does this app decide when you see a card again?
points: Five boxes, shown as foils from Plain to Full Art
Got it moves a card up one box, but only when it was due
Not yet sends it back to box 1, and it returns tomorrow
Harder rarities wait less, so you see them more often
Spacing reviews out beats cramming (the spacing effect)
cards.weakness: Why does reviewing just before you forget work so well?

points: Memories fade along a forgetting curve
Recalling something just as it is fading takes effort
That effort strengthens the memory more than easy repetition
Each successful review flattens the curve, so gaps can grow

cards.title: Row Level Security
cards.question: What is Row Level Security in Postgres, and how does Supabase use it?
points: Policies on a table decide which rows each user can see or change
USING filters reads; WITH CHECK validates writes
auth.uid() comes from the user's JWT
That is why the publishable key can be public
Wrap auth.uid() in a SELECT so it is evaluated once per query
cards.weakness: Why does an UPDATE policy also need WITH CHECK?

points: USING only filters which existing rows you can update
WITH CHECK validates the row after the change
Without it, a user could set user_id to someone else's id
The row would move into another user's data

cards.title: Supabase vs Firebase
cards.question: Why did you build this app on Supabase instead of Firebase?
points: Supabase is Postgres: SQL, joins, constraints, RLS
Firebase Firestore is a NoSQL document store
Supabase is open source and self-hostable: low lock-in
Firebase has built-in offline sync and never pauses
SQL skills carry over to almost any backend job
cards.weakness: How would you add offline support to this app?

points: Cache cards and progress in IndexedDB
Queue answers while offline and send them when back online
Make answers idempotent so resending is safe
The service worker caches the app shell

cards.title: The Streak Query
cards.question: Write the SQL that computes a daily streak from a table of pack openings.
points: Get the distinct local dates with at least one opening
Gaps and islands: date minus row_number() is constant for consecutive days
Group by that value to get each run of days
Take the run that ends today or yesterday
Its length is the current streak
cards.weakness: How do time zones break a naive streak query?

points: Server dates are usually UTC, not the user's day
A pack at 11 p.m. in New York counts as tomorrow in UTC
Streaks then break or double for no reason
Convert to the user's time zone before taking the date
ex.answer: (opened_at at time zone p_tz)::date

cards.title: Definer vs Invoker
cards.question: SECURITY DEFINER vs SECURITY INVOKER functions in Postgres?
points: Definer runs with the function owner's rights and bypasses RLS
Invoker runs as the caller, so RLS still applies
Definer functions in an exposed schema can be called by anyone
Prefer invoker; if you need definer, check auth.uid() inside
Always set search_path on functions
cards.weakness: Why set search_path on a function?

points: Unqualified names are looked up along the search_path
A caller could create an object with the same name in a schema they control
The function would then use the attacker's object
Set search_path to empty and qualify everything (public.cards)

cards.title: PWA
cards.question: What makes a web app a Progressive Web App?
points: A web manifest: name, icons, standalone display
A service worker for caching and offline
Served over HTTPS
Installable to the home screen like a native app
cards.weakness: What can a service worker do that a normal page cannot?

points: Intercept network requests and serve from a cache
Work offline
Run in the background: push notifications, background sync
It is a proxy between the page and the network

cards.title: The Card Flip
cards.question: How does the 3D card flip in this app work?
points: perspective on the parent gives depth
transform-style: preserve-3d keeps children in 3D space
backface-visibility: hidden hides each face when turned away
The back face starts rotated 180 degrees
Rotating the container shows one face, then the other
cards.weakness: Why animate transform instead of width or top?

points: transform and opacity can be animated by the GPU compositor
Changing width or top forces layout and repaint every frame
Layout work causes dropped frames, especially on phones
Smooth 60 fps animations stick to transform and opacity

cards.title: The Pack Builder
cards.question: How does the pack builder pick cards, and why do hard cards show up more?
points: Ten slots: 4 Common, 3 Uncommon, 2 Review, 1 Rare
Each slot takes due cards of its rarity first, then new ones
Review slots take cards you have seen that are due, of any rarity
The Rare slot is an EX 1 time in 5, once its base card reaches Gold
Falls back to other rarities when a slot runs dry
cards.weakness: How would you test the pack builder?

points: Run open_packs inside a transaction as a fake user, then roll back
Assert slot rarities, no duplicate cards, and that due cards come first
Seed progress to cover edge cases: empty sets, everything due, EX unlocked
Tools like pgTAP make these database unit tests

cards.title: TS Types
cards.question: TypeScript: interface vs type, and what is a generic?
points: Both describe object shapes
Interfaces can be extended and merged
Type aliases also handle unions, intersections and mapped types
Generics are type parameters: function first<T>(items: T[]): T
Prefer unknown over any: it forces you to check before use
cards.weakness: unknown vs any?

points: any turns type checking off: anything goes, silently
unknown accepts any value but must be narrowed before use
Use unknown for JSON, catch errors and other outside data
any spreads: once in, it leaks into everything it touches

cards.title: Narrowing
cards.question: What are discriminated unions and type narrowing?
points: A union where every member has a shared literal field, like kind
Checking that field (switch or if) narrows to one member
Exhaustiveness: assign the leftover to never to catch missed cases
Other guards: typeof, in, instanceof
Custom guards: function isOrder(x): x is Order
cards.weakness: How do you make the compiler catch a switch that misses a case?

points: In the default branch, assign the value to a never variable
If a new union member is added, it is no longer never, so the build fails
assertNever also throws at runtime for safety

cards.title: Closures
cards.question: What is a closure? Give a real use.
points: A function remembers variables from the scope where it was created
Private state and factory functions
Event handlers and callbacks
Memoization caches
In React, closures cause stale state bugs
cards.weakness: What is a stale closure in React, and how do you fix it?

points: A callback captures state from the render it was created in
Later renders update state, but the old callback still sees the old value
Common in setInterval and event listeners set up once in useEffect
Fix: functional updates (setX(x => x + 1)), correct deps, or a ref

cards.title: Promise Combinators
cards.question: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?
points: all: resolves when all succeed, rejects on the first failure
allSettled: waits for every promise and reports each status
race: settles with whichever settles first
any: resolves with the first success
For 300,000 items, limit concurrency (batches or p-limit)
cards.weakness: How do you run 10,000 API calls but only 10 at a time?

points: Run a fixed number of workers that each pull the next item
Or use a library like p-limit
Batching with Promise.all on chunks works, but waits for the slowest in each chunk

cards.title: map, filter, reduce
cards.question: Total of paid orders, using filter and reduce.
cards.answer:
const total = orders
  .filter((o) => o.status === 'paid')
  .reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0)
points: map transforms each item, same length out
filter keeps items that pass a test
reduce folds a list into one value; always pass the initial value
cards.weakness: When is reduce the wrong tool?

points: When a plain loop or a simpler method reads more clearly
Building objects with spread in reduce is O(n²): it copies every time
Use Object.groupBy, a Map, or a for...of loop instead
Readability beats cleverness in code reviews

cards.title: == vs ===
cards.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
cards.answer:
0 == ''          // true
null == undefined // true
NaN === NaN       // false
points: === compares without converting types
== converts types first, with surprising rules
Default to ===; == null is a common exception for null or undefined
cards.weakness: What does Object.is do differently from ===?

points: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true; NaN === NaN is false
Object.is(0, -0) is false; 0 === -0 is true
Otherwise the same as ===
React uses Object.is to decide if state changed

cards.title: var, let, const
cards.question: var vs let vs const?
points: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined
let and const are block-scoped
Using let/const before declaration throws (temporal dead zone)
const stops reassignment, not mutation of objects
cards.weakness: Why does a var loop with setTimeout print the same number every time?

points: var creates one variable shared by every iteration
The callbacks run after the loop ends, when i is already 3
let creates a fresh binding per iteration, so each callback keeps its own i

cards.title: Utility Types
cards.question: Partial, Pick, Omit and Record: what does each one do?
cards.answer:
type Draft = Partial<User>
type Public = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>
type Safe = Omit<User, 'password'>
type Counts = Record<Status, number>
points: Partial: every property optional
Pick / Omit: keep or drop listed keys
Record: an object type from a key type and a value type
cards.weakness: How would you write Partial yourself?

points: A mapped type loops over every key with [K in keyof T]
The ? modifier makes each one optional
-? removes it again, which is how Required works

cards.title: this
cards.question: Why does this lose its value when you pass a method as a callback?
points: this is set by how a function is called, not where it is defined
Arrow functions have no own this; they use the surrounding one
cards.weakness: What do call, apply and bind do?

points: call(thisArg, a, b): calls now with this set, arguments listed
apply(thisArg, [a, b]): the same, arguments as an array
bind(thisArg): returns a new function with this fixed for later
ex.answer:
const hi = user.hi.bind(user)
hi()  // 'G'

cards.title: async Errors
cards.question: How do you handle errors with async/await, and what is a common mistake?
points: Wrap awaits in try/catch, or .catch() the promise
fetch only rejects on network errors: check res.ok yourself
Forgetting await means the error escapes the try block
cards.weakness: What happens to an unhandled promise rejection in Node?

points: Since Node 15 the process crashes by default
The unhandledRejection event lets you log it before exiting
Treat it as a bug to fix, not something to swallow
Restart the process (PM2, Kubernetes) rather than limping on

cards.title: Generics
cards.question: Write a typed get(obj, key) that only accepts real keys and returns the right type.
points: keyof T is the union of T's keys
K extends keyof T restricts key to real keys
T[K] is the type of that key's value
cards.weakness: What does extends mean inside a generic?

points: It is a constraint: the type argument must be assignable to it
K extends string means K can be any string literal type
In a conditional type, T extends X ? A : B is a type-level if
Same keyword, two jobs: constrain or test

cards.title: as const
cards.question: Get a union type of the values in this object.
points: as const keeps literal types and makes everything readonly
typeof in a type position turns a value into its type
keyof plus indexed access gives the value union
cards.weakness: Why do many teams avoid TypeScript enums?

points: Enums are one of the few TS features that emit runtime code
Numeric enums accept any number, which hides bugs
They do not work with type-stripping tools (erasableSyntaxOnly)
An as const object plus a union type does the same job

cards.title: infer
cards.question: Write ElementOf<T>: the item type for arrays, T itself otherwise.
cards.answer:
type ElementOf<T> =
  T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T

type A = ElementOf<string[]> // string
type B = ElementOf<number>   // number
points: Conditional type: T extends X ? A : B
infer captures a type from inside the match
cards.weakness: What is a distributive conditional type?

points: When T is a bare type parameter and receives a union, the condition runs per member
ElementOf<string[] | number> gives string | number
Wrap both sides in brackets, [T] extends [X], to stop it

cards.title: Re-renders
cards.question: What triggers a React re-render, and how do you avoid unnecessary ones?
points: Triggers: state change, parent re-render, context value change
Reconciliation diffs the new tree against the old; keys identify list items
memo, useMemo and useCallback skip work when inputs are unchanged
Keep state close to where it is used; split big contexts
React Compiler can memoize automatically
cards.weakness: Why is an array index a bad key?

points: React uses keys to match items between renders
Insert or delete in the middle and every index after it shifts
React then reuses the wrong component, so state and inputs end up on the wrong row
Use a stable id from the data; an index is fine only for static lists

cards.title: useEffect
cards.question: What is useEffect for, and what are common mistakes?
points: Syncing with things outside React: subscriptions, timers, fetching, the DOM
The dependency array controls when it re-runs
Return a cleanup function to undo the effect
Mistake: computing derived state in an effect instead of during render
Mistake: missing dependencies, or loops that set state every run
cards.weakness: Why does my effect run twice in development?

points: React StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts components in development
It is checking that your effect cleans up properly
Production runs it once
If running twice breaks something, the effect is missing a cleanup

cards.title: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR
cards.question: In Next.js, what are CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR, and when do you use each?
points: CSR: the browser renders; slower first paint and weaker SEO
SSR: the server renders each request; always fresh
SSG: HTML built once at build time; fastest
ISR: static pages re-generated in the background on a timer
App Router adds React Server Components
cards.weakness: What is hydration?

points: The server sends ready-made HTML so the page shows quickly
Hydration: React then attaches event handlers and state to that HTML in the browser
Until it finishes, the page is visible but not interactive
If server and client render differently, React warns of a hydration mismatch

cards.title: Do I Need Redux?
cards.question: When do you need Redux instead of React state or context?
points: Local state for local concerns
Context for rarely-changing globals: theme, current user
Redux Toolkit for complex shared state, devtools and middleware
Server data is often better in a fetching library like TanStack Query
Redux: one store, actions, pure reducers
cards.weakness: Why must reducers be pure?

points: Redux detects changes by comparing references, so you must return new objects
Same input must give the same output for time-travel debugging and replay
No side effects (API calls, randomness) inside reducers
Redux Toolkit uses Immer so you can write mutating code safely

cards.title: Vue vs React
cards.question: Vue 3 vs React: what are the key differences?
points: Vue tracks reactive dependencies with proxies and updates only what changed
React re-runs components and diffs the output
Vue uses templates by default; React uses JSX
Vue's setup() runs once; React hooks run on every render
Both are component-based with similar ecosystems
cards.weakness: How does Vue's reactivity know what to update?

points: Vue wraps state in Proxies
Reading a property while rendering records it as a dependency
Writing to it notifies only the components that read it
So Vue updates precisely, with no manual memoization

cards.title: Tailwind CSS
cards.question: What is Tailwind, and what is the main criticism of it?
points: Utility-first: small single-purpose classes like p-4 and flex
A design scale keeps spacing and colours consistent
Only the classes you use end up in the CSS
Criticism: long class lists in markup
Fix: extract repeated patterns into components
cards.weakness: How do you avoid repeating the same long class list everywhere?

points: Extract a component: the classes live in one place
Use a variants helper (cva) for size and color variations
@apply in CSS for small shared patterns, sparingly
Design tokens in the Tailwind theme keep values consistent

cards.title: useState
cards.question: What does useState return, and when do you use the updater form?
points: Returns the current value and a setter
Calling the setter schedules a re-render
Use the updater form when the new value depends on the old one
cards.weakness: Why doesn't state change right after you call setState?

points: State is a snapshot for this render; the setter schedules the next render
Reading the variable right after still gives the old value
Several updates in one event are batched into one render
Use the updater form, or compute the new value in a variable first

cards.title: useRef
cards.question: What are the two main uses of useRef?
points: Hold a reference to a DOM element
Keep a mutable value across renders (a timer id, the previous value)
Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render
cards.weakness: useRef or useState: how do you decide?

points: Does the screen need to update when it changes? Then state
If not (timer ids, latest values for callbacks), a ref
Never read refs during render for display: they do not trigger updates

cards.title: useMemo & useCallback
cards.question: useMemo vs useCallback: what does each keep between renders?
points: useMemo keeps a computed value until its dependencies change
useCallback keeps the same function instance
Both matter mainly for expensive work or memoized children
cards.weakness: When does useMemo make things slower?

points: It has its own cost: storing the value and comparing dependencies
For cheap calculations that cost is bigger than the saving
Unstable dependencies (new objects each render) defeat it entirely
Measure with the Profiler before memoizing; React Compiler can do it for you

cards.title: useContext
cards.question: What problem does Context solve, and how do you use it?
points: Passes data deep without threading props through every level
Good for low-frequency globals: theme, current user, locale
cards.weakness: Why does every consumer re-render when the context value changes?

points: Consumers subscribe to the whole value, not to the parts they read
A new object as value each render re-renders everyone
Memoize the value, and split big contexts into smaller ones
For frequently changing shared state, use a store with selectors

cards.title: useReducer
cards.question: Write a small useReducer for a cart with add and remove actions.
points: State changes are described as actions, handled in one pure function
cards.weakness: useReducer or useState: when do you pick each?

points: useState for independent, simple values
useReducer when several values change together or updates are complex
Reducers are easy to unit-test because they are pure
dispatch is stable, so passing it down never re-renders children

cards.title: Custom Hooks
cards.question: Write a useDebounce hook.
points: A custom hook is a function starting with use that calls other hooks
It shares logic, not state: each caller gets its own
cards.weakness: What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist?

points: Only call hooks at the top level: never in loops, conditions or nested functions
Only call them from components or other hooks
React matches hook state by call order on every render
A conditional hook shifts that order and mixes up state

cards.title: Server Components
cards.question: Server components vs client components in the Next.js App Router?
points: Server components run only on the server: no JS shipped for them
They can fetch data and read secrets directly
Client components ('use client') add interactivity: state, effects, events
Keep client components small, at the leaves of the tree
cards.weakness: Why can't a server component use useState?

points: It renders once on the server and never re-renders in the browser
There is no browser instance to hold state or run effects
Its output is sent as a serialized tree, not live code
Move the interactive part into a client component

cards.title: 10,000 Rows
cards.question: A table with 10,000 rows is janky to scroll and type into. How do you fix it?
points: Profile first: React DevTools Profiler shows what re-renders
Virtualize: render only the rows on screen (TanStack Virtual, react-window)
Memoize rows and keep props stable so one change does not re-render all
Stable keys from data ids
Move filtering off the typing path with useDeferredValue or debouncing
cards.weakness: How does list virtualization work?

points: Only the rows in (and just around) the viewport are rendered
A tall spacer keeps the scrollbar the right size
On scroll, it computes which rows are visible and swaps them in
Variable row heights need measuring, which makes it harder

cards.title: Out-of-Order Results
cards.question: A search box shows results for an older query after you type quickly. Why, and how do you fix it?
points: Each keystroke starts a request; responses arrive in any order
A slow earlier response overwrites the newer one
Cancel stale requests with AbortController in the effect cleanup
Or ignore responses that are not for the latest query
Data libraries (TanStack Query) handle this for you
cards.weakness: How does AbortController cancel a fetch?

points: Pass controller.signal to fetch
controller.abort() rejects the fetch with an AbortError
Abort in the effect cleanup so each new query cancels the old one
Ignore AbortError in the catch

cards.title: Build Autocomplete
cards.question: Design a search autocomplete component. What do you need to get right?
points: Debounce input so you do not fire a request per keystroke
Cancel or ignore stale responses
Cache recent queries; show loading and empty states
Keyboard navigation and ARIA roles (combobox, listbox)
Highlight matches; handle errors without breaking typing
cards.weakness: Debounce vs throttle?

points: Debounce: wait until events stop for N ms, then run once
Throttle: run at most once every N ms while events keep coming
Debounce suits search input
Throttle suits scroll and resize handlers

cards.title: Hydration Mismatch
cards.question: Next.js warns: 'Text content does not match server-rendered HTML'. What causes it, and how do you fix it?
points: The server and the browser rendered different output
Causes: Date.now() or Math.random() in render, checking window, locale formatting
Also invalid HTML nesting, like a div inside a p
Fix: render browser-only values after mount (useEffect), or use useId for ids
cards.weakness: What problem does useId solve?

points: Generates an id that is the same on the server and in the browser
Random or counter-based ids differ between the two and break hydration
Used to link labels and inputs, and ARIA attributes
Not for list keys

cards.title: The Event Loop
cards.question: Explain the Node.js event loop.
points: JavaScript runs on one thread; I/O is non-blocking via libuv
Phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), close
Microtasks (process.nextTick, then promises) run between callbacks
libuv's thread pool handles fs, crypto and DNS work
CPU-heavy code blocks everything: move it to worker threads or a job queue
cards.weakness: In what order do setTimeout(0), setImmediate, Promise.then and process.nextTick run?

points: process.nextTick first: it runs before other microtasks
Then promise callbacks (Promise.then)
Then setTimeout(0) and setImmediate; their order in the main module varies
Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout(0)
ex.answer:
setTimeout(() => log('timeout'))
setImmediate(() => log('immediate'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => log('then'))
process.nextTick(() => log('tick'))
// tick, then, timeout/immediate

cards.title: One Slow Request
cards.question: One CPU-heavy request makes your whole Node API slow. Why, and how do you fix it?
points: It blocks the single event-loop thread, so every request waits
Move the work to worker_threads
Or push it to a background job queue
Or split it into chunks that yield back to the loop
Monitor event-loop lag to catch it
cards.weakness: Cluster mode vs worker threads: what is the difference?

points: Cluster: several Node processes sharing one port; each has its own memory
Scales request handling across CPU cores
Worker threads: threads inside one process, for CPU-heavy tasks
Workers can share memory (SharedArrayBuffer) and pass messages

cards.title: Express Middleware
cards.question: How does Express middleware work?
points: Functions (req, res, next) that run in the order they are registered
next() passes control on; next(err) jumps to error handlers
Error handlers take 4 arguments (err, req, res, next)
Used for parsing, auth, logging, CORS
Express 5 forwards rejected promises; Express 4 needs you to call next(err)
cards.weakness: Give an example where middleware order breaks something.

points: Auth middleware registered after the routes: the routes are unprotected
express.json() after a route: req.body is undefined in it
The error handler must be last, or errors skip it
A catch-all 404 placed early swallows every later route

cards.title: params, query, body
cards.question: In Express, where do req.params, req.query and req.body come from?
points: params: named parts of the path
query: the ?key=value part, always strings
body: the request payload, only with a body parser
cards.weakness: Why is req.body undefined unless you add express.json()?

points: The body arrives as a stream; Express does not read it by default
express.json() reads and parses JSON bodies into req.body
It must be registered before the routes that need it
Set a size limit to avoid huge payloads

cards.title: Streams
cards.question: Why use streams to process a 5 GB file in Node?
cards.answer:
await pipeline(
  fs.createReadStream('in.csv'),
  parseCsv(),
  transformRows(),
  fs.createWriteStream('out.csv'),
)
points: Process data chunk by chunk instead of loading it all into memory
Memory stays flat no matter the file size
pipeline wires streams together and handles errors and cleanup
cards.weakness: What is backpressure?

points: A fast producer can overwhelm a slow consumer
write() returns false when the buffer is full
The producer should pause until the 'drain' event
pipeline and pipe handle this for you

cards.title: CORS
cards.question: Your frontend gets a CORS error calling your API. What is happening?
points: Browsers block reading responses from another origin unless the server allows it
The server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your origin
It is a browser rule: curl and servers are not affected
Fix it on the API, for example with the cors middleware
cards.weakness: What is a preflight request?

points: An OPTIONS request the browser sends before the real one
Triggered by non-simple requests: PUT, DELETE, custom headers, JSON bodies
The server must answer with the allowed methods and headers
Access-Control-Max-Age caches the answer to save round trips

cards.title: The Slow Leak
cards.question: A Node service's memory grows for hours until it crashes. How do you find the leak?
points: Confirm it: graph heap used over time, not just total memory
Take heap snapshots minutes apart and compare what keeps growing
Usual suspects: unbounded caches and maps, event listeners never removed
Also closures holding big objects, and timers never cleared
Fix, then load-test to prove memory stays flat
cards.weakness: What is a WeakMap good for?

points: Keys are objects, held weakly
When the key object is no longer used elsewhere, the entry can be garbage-collected
Good for attaching data to objects you do not own, without leaking
Not iterable and has no size, because entries can vanish

cards.title: Pinned at 100%
cards.question: Your Node API sits at 100% CPU on one core while the server has 8. What is going on, and what do you do?
points: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so one process uses one core
Profile first: is it real load or one hot function?
Run one process per core (cluster, PM2) or more replicas in Kubernetes
Move heavy CPU work to worker threads or a job queue
cards.weakness: How do you profile a Node process in production?

points: --cpu-prof, or attach Chrome DevTools via --inspect
Flame graphs (Clinic.js, 0x) show where time goes
APM tools sample continuously with low overhead
Profile under realistic load, not on an idle box

cards.title: Vite vs Webpack
cards.question: Why is Vite so much faster than Webpack in development?
points: Webpack bundles the whole app before it can serve it
Vite serves native ES modules, and the browser asks for files as needed
Dependencies are pre-bundled once
Hot updates replace only the changed module
Production builds are still bundled for speed
cards.weakness: Why does Vite still bundle for production?

points: Hundreds of small module requests are slow over a real network
Bundling enables tree-shaking, minification and code splitting
Chunks can be cached with content hashes
Vite uses Rollup (now Rolldown) for production builds

cards.title: Jest vs Mocha
cards.question: Jest vs Mocha?
points: Jest: all-in-one runner, assertions, mocks, coverage and snapshots
Mocha: just the runner; add Chai, Sinon and nyc
Jest runs test files in parallel workers
Vitest is the natural pick for Vite projects
cards.weakness: How do you mock a third-party API in Jest?

points: jest.mock the HTTP client module and return fake responses
Or mock fetch / axios per test with mockResolvedValue
Or intercept at the network layer with MSW (Mock Service Worker)
Test errors too: timeouts, 429s, bad payloads
ex.answer:
jest.mock('./amazonClient')
amazonClient.getOrders
  .mockResolvedValue([{ id: '1' }])

cards.title: Bias vs Variance
cards.question: Explain bias vs variance, and overfitting.
points: High bias: too simple, underfits (bad on train and test)
High variance: too complex, overfits (great on train, bad on test)
A big gap between train and validation error signals overfitting
Fixes: more data, regularization (L2, dropout), simpler model, early stopping
Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate
cards.weakness: How do you detect overfitting during training?

points: Plot training and validation loss every epoch
Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises: overfitting
Early stopping halts at the best validation score
A big gap in final train vs validation accuracy says the same

cards.title: Train, Val, Test
cards.question: Why separate train, validation and test sets?
points: Train: fit the model
Validation: tune hyperparameters and choose models
Test: one final, unbiased estimate; touch it once
Data leakage makes results look better than reality
k-fold cross-validation when data is scarce
cards.weakness: Give an example of data leakage.

points: Scaling or imputing using statistics from the whole dataset, before splitting
Features that are only known after the outcome (refund issued, to predict fraud)
Random splits on time series: the model sees the future
The same customer in both train and test sets

cards.title: Precision & Recall
cards.question: Precision, recall and F1: when does accuracy lie?
points: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of what you flagged, how much was right
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of what was there, how much you found
F1 is their harmonic mean
With 99% negatives, predicting all negative scores 99% accuracy
Choose by the cost of false positives vs false negatives
cards.weakness: Spam filter: optimise precision or recall?

points: Usually precision: a real email in spam (false positive) is costly
Some spam getting through is annoying but tolerable
Fraud or cancer screening flip it: missing a case is worse, so recall
Tune the threshold to the cost of each kind of mistake

cards.title: Big-O Basics
cards.question: Big-O of common operations: hash map, sorted array, heap, sorting?
points: Hash map: O(1) average lookup and insert, O(n) worst case
Sorted array: O(log n) binary search, O(n) insert
Heap: O(log n) push and pop, O(1) peek
Comparison sorting: O(n log n)
cards.weakness: When does a hash map degrade to O(n)?

points: When many keys land in the same bucket (collisions)
A poor hash function, or keys crafted to collide (hash flooding attacks)
Lookups then walk a long chain: O(n)
Randomized hashing and resizing keep it O(1) on average

cards.title: sklearn Pipeline
cards.question: Build a scikit-learn pipeline that scales features and fits a classifier.
cards.answer:
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scale', StandardScaler()),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression()),
])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
pipe.predict(X_test)
points: Chains preprocessing and a model into one estimator
fit fits every step in order; predict reuses them
cards.weakness: Why put preprocessing inside the pipeline?

points: Steps are fitted only on training data, so no leakage
Cross-validation refits them per fold correctly
One object to save and deploy, with the exact same transforms
Hyperparameter search can tune preprocessing too

cards.title: Cross-Validation
cards.question: How does k-fold cross-validation work, and why use it?
points: Split data into k folds; train on k-1, validate on the one left out
Repeat k times so every fold is validated once
Average the scores: a steadier estimate than one split
Costs k times the training
cards.weakness: Why use stratified k-fold?

points: It keeps the class balance the same in every fold
With rare classes, a plain split might leave a fold with none
Scores are then more stable and honest
For time series, use time-based splits instead

cards.title: L1 vs L2
cards.question: L1 vs L2 regularization?
points: Both add a penalty on weight size to the loss
L2 (ridge): penalizes squared weights; shrinks them all smoothly
L1 (lasso): penalizes absolute weights; pushes many to exactly zero
Elastic net mixes both
cards.weakness: Why does L1 produce sparse weights?

points: L1's penalty has the same slope however small the weight gets
So it keeps pushing small weights all the way to zero
L2's push fades as the weight shrinks, so weights rarely hit zero
That makes L1 a form of feature selection

cards.title: Imbalanced Data
cards.question: Only 1% of transactions are fraud. How do you train a useful model?
points: Pick the right metric: precision, recall, PR AUC; not accuracy
Class weights so mistakes on the rare class cost more
Resample: oversample the rare class or undersample the common one
Tune the decision threshold to the business cost
cards.weakness: Why can ROC AUC look great on very imbalanced data?

points: It uses the false positive rate, divided by the huge number of negatives
Thousands of false alarms still look like a tiny rate
Precision-recall AUC exposes them
Report PR AUC for rare-event problems

cards.title: Feature Scaling
cards.question: When do you need to scale features, and how?
points: Standardize (mean 0, std 1) or min-max scale to a range
Needed for distance-based and gradient-based models: k-NN, SVM, linear models, neural nets
Tree models (random forest, XGBoost) do not care
Without it, large-valued features dominate
cards.weakness: Why fit the scaler on the training data only?

points: Fitting on everything leaks test-set statistics into training
Scores then look better than real-world performance
Fit on train, then transform validation and test with it
A Pipeline does this automatically

cards.title: Prove It Online
cards.question: A new model beats the old one offline. How do you prove it is better in production?
points: A/B test: random users get old or new, everything else equal
Pick the business metric and sample size before starting
Run long enough to cover weekly patterns
Watch guardrail metrics: latency, errors, complaints
Shadow mode first if a bad model is risky
cards.weakness: What does statistically significant actually mean?

points: If there were really no difference, a result this big would rarely happen by chance
A p-value below 0.05 means under 5% chance under 'no difference'
It does not mean the effect is large or important
Do not peek and stop early: it inflates false positives

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.question: Explain backpropagation and gradient descent.
points: Forward pass computes predictions and the loss
Backprop applies the chain rule to get gradients layer by layer, backwards
Gradient descent moves weights against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate
Mini-batch SGD and Adam in practice
Vanishing gradients: helped by ReLU, residual connections, normalization
cards.weakness: What happens if the learning rate is too high or too low?

points: Too high: loss jumps around or explodes to NaN
Too low: training crawls or gets stuck
Use a learning-rate finder, warmup, and a schedule that decays it
Adam is more forgiving than plain SGD, but still sensitive

cards.title: Attention
cards.question: How does attention work in a Transformer?
points: Tokens become embeddings plus position information
Each token is projected into a query, key and value
Attention = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V: each token weighs every other token
Multi-head: several attention patterns in parallel
Stacked with feed-forward layers, residuals and layer norm; parallel, unlike RNNs
cards.weakness: Why divide by the square root of d?

points: Dot products grow with the vector dimension d
Big values push softmax towards one-hot, where gradients vanish
Dividing by sqrt(d) keeps scores at a stable scale
So training stays stable whatever the model width

cards.title: PyTorch vs TF
cards.question: PyTorch vs TensorFlow?
points: PyTorch: eager and Pythonic; the research default
TensorFlow and Keras: strong production tooling (Serving, Lite)
Both compile graphs when needed (torch.compile, tf.function)
Both export to ONNX
cards.weakness: What does model.eval() change in PyTorch?

points: Switches layers to inference behavior
Dropout turns off; BatchNorm uses its stored running statistics
It does not stop gradients: also wrap inference in torch.no_grad()
Forgetting it gives noisy, worse predictions
ex.answer:
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    preds = model(x)

cards.title: Training Loop
cards.question: Write a basic PyTorch training loop.
cards.answer:
model.train()
for x, y in loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
points: Forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step
model.train() enables dropout and batch-norm updates
cards.weakness: Why call optimizer.zero_grad() every step?

points: PyTorch adds new gradients to the existing ones (accumulates)
Without zeroing, each step uses the sum of all past gradients
Training then behaves wrongly
Skipping it on purpose is how gradient accumulation works

cards.title: Tokenization
cards.question: How do language models split text into tokens?
points: Subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece): common words are one token, rare ones split into pieces
Keeps the vocabulary small while handling any word
Costs and context limits are counted in tokens, not words
Roughly 3 to 4 characters per token in English
cards.weakness: Why do language models struggle to count the letters in a word?

points: The model sees tokens, not letters
A word may be one or two tokens, hiding its spelling
It has to have learned each token's letters indirectly
Splitting the word into characters first helps

cards.title: Dropout & BatchNorm
cards.question: What do dropout and batch normalization do?
points: Dropout: randomly zeroes some activations during training
BatchNorm: normalizes each layer's inputs using batch statistics
BatchNorm speeds up and steadies training
Both behave differently at inference time
cards.weakness: Why does dropout reduce overfitting?

points: No neuron can rely on any one other neuron always being there
The network learns redundant, more general features
Acts like averaging many smaller networks
Turned off at inference, with outputs scaled to match

cards.title: Vanishing Gradients
cards.question: What are vanishing and exploding gradients, and how do you fix them?
points: Backprop multiplies many factors layer by layer
Factors below 1 shrink gradients to nothing: early layers stop learning
Factors above 1 blow them up: loss goes to NaN
Fixes: ReLU, good initialization, normalization, residual connections, gradient clipping
cards.weakness: How do residual connections help?

points: Each block adds its input to its output: x + f(x)
Gradients get a shortcut path straight back through the addition
So signals survive through very deep networks
Why ResNets and Transformers can stack so many layers

cards.title: Keyword vs Dense
cards.question: Information retrieval: BM25 keyword search vs dense embeddings?
points: TF-IDF: term frequency times inverse document frequency
BM25 adds term saturation and document length normalization
Dense embeddings capture meaning; search by nearest neighbour
Hybrid search combines both and is common in practice
Evaluate with precision@k, MAP, nDCG
cards.weakness: When does keyword search beat embeddings?

points: Exact terms: product codes, error messages, names, SKUs
Rare words the embedding model never learned well
When users expect literal matches
Hybrid search combines both and usually wins

cards.title: Model Serving
cards.question: ONNX Runtime, TensorRT and Triton: what does each one do?
points: ONNX: a portable model format; ONNX Runtime runs it on many kinds of hardware
TensorRT: NVIDIA's GPU optimizer (layer fusion, FP16 and INT8)
Triton Inference Server: serves models over HTTP or gRPC
Triton adds dynamic batching and hosts many models at once
Typical path: train in PyTorch, export to ONNX, optimize, serve
cards.weakness: What does quantization trade away?

points: Stores weights in fewer bits: INT8 instead of FP32
Smaller and faster, especially on GPUs and edge devices
Costs some accuracy, usually small
Calibrate on real data and measure accuracy before shipping

cards.title: Embeddings
cards.question: What are embeddings, and what are they used for?
points: Dense vectors where similar items end up close together
Learned from data: words, sentences, products, users
Used for semantic search, recommendations, clustering, deduplication
Compared with cosine similarity, in a vector index
cards.weakness: Cosine similarity vs dot product?

points: Cosine compares direction only; it ignores vector length
Dot product mixes direction and length
For normalized vectors they give the same ranking
Use whatever the embedding model was trained with

cards.title: Recommendations
cards.question: Design a 'customers also bought' recommender for an e-commerce site.
points: Candidates: co-purchase counts, item embeddings, popular items
Ranking: a model scoring candidates with user and item features
Filter out-of-stock and already-bought items; add diversity
Serve precomputed candidates from a fast store; rank online
Measure with an A/B test on clicks and revenue, not just offline accuracy
cards.weakness: What is the cold-start problem?

points: New users and new items have no interaction history
Collaborative filtering cannot score them
Use content features (category, price, text) and popularity
Ask new users for preferences; explore new items deliberately

cards.title: The Model Got Worse
cards.question: A model was accurate at launch, but three months later its predictions are noticeably worse. What do you do?
points: Check the pipeline first: missing features, schema changes, bugs
Compare input distributions now vs training time (drift metrics)
Check if the relationship itself changed, with fresh labels
Retrain on recent data; set up scheduled retraining
Monitor inputs and outputs continuously, not just at launch
cards.weakness: Data drift vs concept drift?

points: Data drift: inputs change (new customer types, new products)
Concept drift: the link from inputs to the answer changes
Example: the same behavior that meant fraud last year no longer does
Data drift is visible without labels; concept drift needs fresh labels

cards.title: RAG over Docs
cards.question: Design a question-answering assistant over your company's internal docs.
points: Ingest: split docs into chunks, embed them, store in a vector index
Query: retrieve the top chunks (hybrid keyword plus vector), rerank them
Prompt an LLM with the chunks; require citations
Respect permissions: only retrieve docs the user may see
Refresh the index when docs change; evaluate answers continuously
cards.weakness: How do you evaluate a RAG system?

points: A test set of real questions with known good answers and sources
Retrieval: did the right chunks come back (recall@k)?
Answer: is it correct and grounded in the retrieved text?
Use LLM-as-judge with spot checks by humans; track it over time

cards.title: Serve It Fast
cards.question: Serve a PyTorch model to thousands of requests per second with low latency. How?
points: Export to ONNX; optimize with TensorRT on NVIDIA GPUs
Quantize (FP16 or INT8) if accuracy holds
Serve with Triton: dynamic batching and several model instances per GPU
Autoscale on queue latency; cache frequent inputs
Measure p99 latency and throughput under realistic load
cards.weakness: What does dynamic batching trade off?

points: It waits briefly to group requests into one batch
GPUs process a batch almost as fast as one item: much higher throughput
Each request may wait a few milliseconds longer
Tune the maximum wait time against your latency target

cards.title: Comprehensions
cards.question: Write a list comprehension of the squares of the even numbers below 10, and a dict comprehension.
cards.answer:
squares = [n * n for n in range(10)
           if n % 2 == 0]
# [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

by_id = {u.id: u for u in users}
points: [expression for item in iterable if condition]
Dict and set comprehensions use the same shape
Clearer and usually faster than an append loop
cards.weakness: List comprehension vs generator expression?

points: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory
A generator expression yields items one at a time, lazily
Use a generator for big data or when you only iterate once
Written with parentheses: sum(n * n for n in nums)

cards.title: *args, **kwargs
cards.question: What do *args and **kwargs do?
points: *args collects extra positional arguments as a tuple
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments as a dict
The same stars unpack when calling: f(*items, **opts)
cards.weakness: What is the mutable default argument trap?

points: Defaults are created once, when the function is defined
A default list is shared across every call
Use None and create the list inside

cards.title: with
cards.question: What does the with statement do?
cards.answer:
with open('orders.csv') as f:
    rows = f.readlines()
# file is closed here, even on error
points: Runs setup, then guarantees cleanup when the block exits
Cleanup runs even if an exception is raised
Used for files, locks, DB transactions, timers
cards.weakness: How do you write your own context manager?

points: A class with __enter__ and __exit__ methods
Or a generator with @contextmanager: code before yield is setup, after is cleanup
Put cleanup in finally so it runs on errors

cards.title: dict Tools
cards.question: Count orders per status, and group order ids by seller.
points: Counter counts things; most_common(n) ranks them
defaultdict creates missing keys automatically
dict.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError
cards.weakness: Why must dictionary keys be hashable?

points: Dicts find keys by their hash, in O(1) on average
If a key changed after insertion, its hash would change and it would be lost
So keys must be immutable: str, int, tuple of immutables
Lists and dicts cannot be keys

cards.title: is vs ==
cards.question: What is the difference between is and == in Python?
cards.answer:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
a == b   # True: same contents
a is b   # False: different objects
x is None  # the right way
points: == compares values
is compares identity: the same object in memory
Use is only for None, True and False
cards.weakness: Why does a is b sometimes work for small integers?

points: CPython caches integers from -5 to 256
So small ints with the same value are the same object
Outside that range, equal ints can be different objects
An implementation detail: never rely on it

cards.title: Decorators
cards.question: Write a decorator that logs how long a function takes.
points: A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapped one
cards.weakness: Why use functools.wraps?

points: Without it, the wrapper replaces the function's name and docstring
Debugging, logging and docs then show 'wrapper'
wraps copies __name__, __doc__ and other metadata
It also sets __wrapped__ so tools can find the original

cards.title: Generators
cards.question: Read a huge file in batches of 1,000 lines without loading it all.
points: yield pauses the function and hands back a value
Memory stays small: only one batch at a time
cards.weakness: What does yield from do?

points: Delegates to another iterable or generator
Yields every value it produces, as if inline
Also passes through send() and the sub-generator's return value
Handy for recursive generators like walking a tree

cards.title: The GIL
cards.question: What is the GIL, and how does it affect Python performance?
points: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time
Threads still help for I/O: the GIL is released while waiting
CPU-heavy Python code does not speed up with threads
NumPy and PyTorch release it inside their C code; Python 3.13+ has an optional free-threaded build
cards.weakness: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio?

points: threading: concurrent I/O with simple code; limited by the GIL for CPU work
multiprocessing: separate processes, true parallel CPU work, more memory
asyncio: one thread, thousands of concurrent I/O tasks, needs async libraries
CPU-bound: processes. Lots of I/O: asyncio. Some I/O: threads

cards.title: asyncio
cards.question: Fetch 100 URLs concurrently with asyncio, at most 10 at a time.
cards.answer:
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def fetch(client, url):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(url)
        return r.json()

async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        *(fetch(c, u) for u in urls))
points: gather runs coroutines concurrently; a Semaphore caps it
cards.weakness: What happens if you call a blocking function inside async code?

points: It blocks the whole event loop: every other task freezes
Examples: time.sleep, requests.get, heavy CPU work
Use async libraries (asyncio.sleep, httpx)
Or offload it: await asyncio.to_thread(fn)

cards.title: Type Hints
cards.question: Type a function and define a typed record with a dataclass.
points: Hints are not enforced at runtime; mypy or pyright check them
dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you
cards.weakness: dataclass vs a Pydantic model?

points: dataclass: plain containers, no validation, standard library
Pydantic: validates and converts input at runtime
Use Pydantic at boundaries: API input, config, JSON
Dataclasses inside your code, where data is already trusted

cards.title: Broadcasting
cards.question: Subtract each column's mean from a matrix without a loop.
cards.answer:
X = np.random.rand(100, 3)   # (100, 3)
means = X.mean(axis=0)       # (3,)
X_centered = X - means       # broadcasts
points: NumPy stretches smaller arrays to match shapes, without copying
Shapes are compared from the right
Vectorized code is far faster than Python loops
cards.weakness: When does broadcasting fail?

points: Each dimension, compared from the right, must be equal or 1
Add an axis to fix it: means[:, None] or reshape(-1, 1)
ex.answer:
row_means = X.mean(axis=1)    # (100,)
X - row_means[:, None]        # (100, 1)

cards.title: reshape & axis
cards.question: What do reshape(-1, 1) and sum(axis=0) do?
cards.answer:
a = np.arange(6)        # (6,)
m = a.reshape(2, 3)     # (2, 3)
m.sum(axis=0)  # [3, 5, 7]  columns
m.sum(axis=1)  # [3, 12]    rows
a.reshape(-1, 1)        # (6, 1)
points: reshape changes the shape without copying data (when it can)
-1 means: work this dimension out for me
cards.weakness: What does axis=0 vs axis=1 actually mean?

points: The axis you name is the one that collapses
axis=0 runs down the rows: one result per column
axis=1 runs across the columns: one result per row
Same rule in pandas: df.mean(axis=0) gives column means

cards.title: loc vs iloc
cards.question: loc vs iloc in pandas?
cards.answer:
df.loc[df.total > 100, ['id', 'total']]
df.iloc[0:5, 0:2]   # first 5 rows, 2 cols
points: loc selects by labels and boolean masks
iloc selects by integer positions
loc slices include the end label; iloc slices exclude it
cards.weakness: What is SettingWithCopyWarning?

points: You assigned to something that may be a copy of the original
Chained indexing like df[mask]['col'] = 0 may not change df
Use one .loc call: df.loc[mask, 'col'] = 0
Or call .copy() if you want a separate frame

cards.title: groupby
cards.question: Revenue and order count per seller, highest revenue first.
cards.answer:
(df.groupby('seller')
   .agg(revenue=('total', 'sum'),
        orders=('id', 'count'))
   .sort_values('revenue',
                ascending=False))
points: Split by a key, apply a function, combine the results
Named aggregation gives clean column names
cards.weakness: groupby with agg vs transform?

points: agg returns one row per group
transform returns a value for every original row, same length as df
Use transform to add group statistics as a column
ex.answer:
df['seller_avg'] = (
    df.groupby('seller')['total']
      .transform('mean'))

cards.title: merge
cards.question: Join orders to customers in pandas, keeping all orders.
cards.answer:
df = orders.merge(
    customers,
    left_on='customer_id',
    right_on='id',
    how='left',
    validate='many_to_one',
)
points: Works like SQL joins: how='inner', 'left', 'right', 'outer'
validate catches unexpected duplicate keys
Check row counts before and after
cards.weakness: merge vs join vs concat?

points: merge: SQL-style join on columns
join: a shortcut for merging on the index
concat: stack frames on top of each other or side by side
Joining finds matching rows; concat just glues

cards.title: 20 GB CSV
cards.question: pandas runs out of memory loading a 20 GB CSV. What are your options?
points: Read only the columns you need (usecols) with smaller dtypes
Process it in chunks (chunksize) and aggregate as you go
Convert to Parquet once: columnar and compressed
Use tools built for it: Polars, DuckDB, or Spark for really big data
cards.weakness: Why does the category dtype save so much memory?

points: Repeated strings are stored once, in a lookup table
Each row keeps a small integer code instead of a full string
A status column with millions of rows shrinks hugely
Group-bys on it get faster too

cards.title: Indexes
cards.question: How does a database index work, and what does it cost?
points: Usually a B-tree: a sorted structure, so lookups are O(log n) instead of a full scan
Composite index column order matters (leftmost prefix rule)
Costs: slower writes and extra storage
Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Partial and covering indexes for special cases
cards.weakness: With an index on (a, b), does WHERE b = ? use it?

points: Usually no: a B-tree on (a, b) is sorted by a first, so b on its own is scattered
Leftmost prefix: filters on a, or on a and b, can use it
Postgres 18+ can skip-scan it when a has only a few distinct values
Fix: add an index on (b), or reorder to (b, a) if that matches your queries
ex.answer:
-- index on (a, b)
WHERE a = 1            -- uses it
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2  -- uses it
WHERE b = 2            -- usually not

cards.title: ACID & Isolation
cards.question: What does ACID mean, and what are isolation levels?
points: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable
Read committed is Postgres's default
Repeatable read and serializable are stricter
Anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks rows you are about to change
cards.weakness: What is a phantom read?

points: A query runs twice in one transaction and the second run returns new rows
Another transaction inserted rows matching your WHERE in between
Prevented by serializable isolation (and by repeatable read in Postgres)
Different from a non-repeatable read, where an existing row changed

cards.title: The Last Unit
cards.question: One unit left, two orders at the same instant. Design it so you never oversell.
points: Atomic conditional update: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0
Check rows affected: 0 means sold out
Or lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction
Or optimistic locking with a version column
Across marketplaces: keep a safety buffer and sync stock quickly
cards.weakness: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when do you use each?

points: Pessimistic: lock the row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE); safe under heavy contention
Optimistic: read a version, update WHERE version = ?, retry if 0 rows changed
Optimistic is cheaper when conflicts are rare
Pessimistic avoids retry storms when conflicts are common, but holds locks
ex.answer:
UPDATE stock
SET qty = qty - 1, version = version + 1
WHERE sku = $1 AND version = $2;
-- 0 rows: someone else won, retry

cards.title: 300k Upserts
cards.question: Syncing 300,000 SKUs into Postgres: how do you write that efficiently?
points: Batch writes (multi-row INSERT or COPY), never row by row
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE for upserts
Skip unchanged rows (compare a hash or updated_at)
Commit in chunks of a few thousand rows
A unique index on the conflict key
cards.weakness: Why not do all 300,000 rows in one giant transaction?

points: Holds locks for the whole run, blocking other writers
One failure near the end rolls back everything
Huge WAL and memory use, and long replication lag
Chunks of a few thousand give progress, retries and room for other work

cards.title: Pagination
cards.question: Offset vs cursor pagination?
points: OFFSET scans and throws away rows, so deep pages get slow
Offsets also skip or repeat rows when data changes
Cursor (keyset): WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n
Fast and stable with an index
Trade-off: no jumping straight to page 50
cards.weakness: How do you build a cursor when sorting by a non-unique column like created_at?

points: Add a unique tie-breaker, usually the id
Order by (created_at, id) and filter with a row comparison
Index (created_at, id) so it stays fast
ex.answer:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

cards.title: COALESCE
cards.question: What does COALESCE do? Show it in a query.
points: Returns the first argument that is not NULL
Common for fallbacks and display defaults
Arguments must be of compatible types
cards.weakness: COALESCE vs NULLIF: what does each do?

points: COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first value that is not NULL
NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, otherwise a
Classic combo: avoid dividing by zero
ex.answer:
SELECT total / NULLIF(items, 0)
FROM orders;  -- NULL instead of error

cards.title: JOIN Types
cards.question: Name the four main JOIN types and what each one keeps.
points: INNER: only rows that match on both sides
LEFT: every left row, NULLs where the right has no match
RIGHT: every right row, NULLs where the left has no match
FULL: every row from both sides
cards.weakness: What does a CROSS JOIN produce, and when is it useful?

points: Every row of the left table paired with every row of the right
