Result size is rows(A) × rows(B), so it explodes fast
Useful to generate combinations: every product with every size
Also to fill gaps, e.g. a calendar of days crossed with stores

cards.title: SELECT *
cards.question: Why is SELECT * a bad habit in production code?
points: Fetches columns you do not need: more I/O and network
Stops the database using a covering index
A schema change silently changes what your code receives
Fine for quick exploration, not for application queries
cards.weakness: What is a covering index?

points: An index that contains every column a query needs
The database answers from the index alone (index-only scan)
Postgres: INCLUDE adds extra columns without making them keys
SELECT * usually defeats it, because no index has every column
ex.answer:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id)
  INCLUDE (total, status);

cards.title: MVCC
cards.question: How does Postgres let readers and writers work at the same time without blocking each other?
points: MVCC: an UPDATE writes a new row version instead of overwriting
Each transaction reads from a snapshot of committed versions
So readers never wait for writers, and writers never wait for readers
Old versions are cleaned up later by VACUUM
cards.weakness: What happens when VACUUM cannot keep up?

points: Dead row versions pile up: tables and indexes bloat and queries slow down
Long-running transactions stop VACUUM from removing old versions
Worst case: transaction ID wraparound, where Postgres stops accepting writes to protect data
Fix: tune autovacuum, kill idle-in-transaction sessions, watch dead tuples

cards.title: 20 ms to 5 s
cards.question: A query that took 20 ms now takes 5 seconds. Walk me through what you check.
points: EXPLAIN ANALYZE: did the plan change, for example to a sequential scan?
Stale statistics after data growth: run ANALYZE
Missing or unused index for the current filter
Locks: is it waiting? Check pg_stat_activity and pg_locks
Resources: CPU, disk I/O, connection pool saturation
cards.weakness: How do you find which queries are slowest across the whole database?

points: pg_stat_statements: total and mean time per normalized query
Sort by total time to find what costs the most overall
Slow query log (log_min_duration_statement) for outliers
APM traces show which endpoints trigger them
ex.answer:
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

cards.title: 10x the Reads
cards.question: Reads on your Postgres database grow 10x. What are your options, in the order you would try them?
points: Fix queries and indexes first: cheapest and often enough
Cache hot reads in Redis
Connection pooling (PgBouncer) to stop connection overload
Read replicas, accepting replication lag
Partitioning, and sharding only as a last resort
cards.weakness: What is replication lag, and how can it bite your users?

points: Replicas apply the primary's changes a little later, from milliseconds to seconds
A user saves something, the next read hits a replica, and the change is not there
Fix: read your own writes from the primary for a short window
Or route by session, and monitor lag so stale replicas are taken out

cards.title: GROUP BY & HAVING
cards.question: List customers with more than 5 orders, with their order count.
cards.answer:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
points: WHERE filters rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after aggregation
Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE
cards.weakness: In what order does SQL actually evaluate a query's clauses?

points: FROM and JOINs, then WHERE
GROUP BY, then HAVING
SELECT, then DISTINCT
ORDER BY, then LIMIT / OFFSET
That is why a SELECT alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE

cards.title: Three COUNTs
cards.question: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) vs COUNT(DISTINCT column): what does each count?
points: COUNT(*): every row
COUNT(column): rows where that column is not NULL
COUNT(DISTINCT column): unique non-NULL values
Mixing them up silently gives wrong totals
cards.weakness: Why can COUNT(*) on a huge Postgres table be slow?

points: MVCC: each transaction may see a different set of rows
So Postgres cannot keep one stored row count; it must scan
For a rough number, read reltuples from pg_class
Or keep a counter table, or count a filtered, indexed subset

cards.title: = NULL
cards.question: Why does WHERE status = NULL always return zero rows?
cards.answer: WHERE status IS NULL
points: NULL means unknown, so NULL = NULL is unknown, not true
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
COALESCE swaps NULLs for a fallback value
cards.weakness: Why is NOT IN dangerous when the list can contain NULL?

points: x NOT IN (1, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> NULL
x <> NULL is unknown, so the whole condition is never true
The query quietly returns no rows
Use NOT EXISTS instead, which handles NULLs correctly

cards.title: LIKE & ILIKE
cards.question: Find customers whose name starts with 'gau', ignoring case.
cards.answer:
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE name ILIKE 'gau%';
points: % matches any run of characters, _ matches exactly one
LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is not (Postgres)
A prefix pattern ('gau%') can use a suitable index
cards.weakness: Why is LIKE '%abc' slow, and how do you speed it up?

points: A leading wildcard cannot use a normal B-tree index, so it scans
Postgres pg_trgm extension plus a GIN trigram index fixes it
For real search, use full-text search (tsvector) instead

cards.title: Keys & Constraints
cards.question: Primary key vs foreign key vs unique constraint?
points: Primary key: identifies each row; unique and not NULL; one per table
Foreign key: a column must match a key in another table
Unique: no duplicates, but NULLs are allowed
All three are enforced by the database, not just the app
cards.weakness: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do, and when is it dangerous?

points: Deleting a parent row deletes all rows that reference it
Handy for owned data: delete an order, delete its line items
Dangerous when chains are long: one delete can wipe far more than expected
Alternatives: RESTRICT (block the delete) or soft deletes

cards.title: Latest per Group
cards.question: Get each customer's most recent order using a window function.
points: Window functions look at related rows without collapsing them
You cannot filter a window result in the same WHERE, so wrap it
cards.weakness: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?

points: ROW_NUMBER: always 1, 2, 3, even when values tie
RANK: ties share a number, then it skips (1, 1, 3)
DENSE_RANK: ties share a number, no gaps (1, 1, 2)
Pick based on whether ties should both count

cards.title: CTEs
cards.question: Using a CTE, find customers who spent over 1000 in total.
cards.answer:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
    SUM(total) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM spend
WHERE total > 1000;
points: WITH names a subquery so the query reads top to bottom
You can chain several CTEs, each using the ones before
cards.weakness: When would you use WITH RECURSIVE?

points: To walk hierarchies: category trees, org charts, threaded comments
An anchor query, UNION ALL, then a part that references itself
Stops when the recursive part returns no rows
Guard against cycles with a depth limit

cards.title: Reading EXPLAIN
cards.question: You run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. What do you look for?
points: Seq Scan on a big table that returns few rows: likely a missing index
Estimated vs actual rows: a big gap means stale statistics
The node with the most time; work from there
Nested loops over large inputs, and sorts spilling to disk
cards.weakness: Why might Postgres ignore an index that exists?

points: The query returns a large share of the table, so a scan is cheaper
The index does not match: wrong column order, or a function on the column
A type mismatch or implicit cast in the comparison
Stale statistics make the planner misjudge; run ANALYZE

cards.title: Deadlocks
cards.question: What is a deadlock, and how do you avoid one?
points: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so both wait forever
The database detects it and aborts one of them
Avoid it: always lock rows in the same order
Keep transactions short, and retry the aborted one
cards.weakness: Two transfers between accounts A and B deadlock. How do you fix it?

points: One transfer locks A then B, the other locks B then A
Always lock the lower account id first, whatever the direction
Or take both locks in one statement, ordered by id
Retry on a deadlock error as a safety net
ex.answer:
SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE id IN ($1, $2)
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE;

cards.title: VACUUM
cards.question: What does VACUUM do in Postgres, and what is autovacuum?
points: Removes dead row versions left behind by MVCC
Makes the space reusable and updates the visibility map
Autovacuum runs it automatically based on how much a table changes
VACUUM FULL rewrites the table to shrink it, but locks it
cards.weakness: Why is VACUUM FULL risky on a production table?

points: It takes an exclusive lock: no reads or writes until it finishes
It needs enough free disk to write a full copy
On a big table that can mean a long outage
Use pg_repack, or fix autovacuum so bloat does not build up

cards.title: JSONB
cards.question: When would you store data as JSONB in Postgres, and when not?
points: Good for flexible attributes that vary per row (marketplace product specs)
Queryable with ->, ->> and @>, and indexable with GIN
Bad for fields you filter, join or constrain on all the time
No foreign keys or column types inside it
cards.weakness: How do you index a JSONB column for containment queries?

points: A GIN index supports @> (contains) queries
jsonb_path_ops makes it smaller and faster, for @> only
For one hot key, an expression index on that key is better

cards.title: Connection Pools
cards.question: Why do you need a connection pool for Postgres?
points: Each Postgres connection is a whole process, so connections are expensive
Opening one per request adds latency and can exhaust max_connections
A pool keeps a few connections open and lends them out
Many app servers? Add PgBouncer in front of the database
cards.weakness: PgBouncer in transaction mode breaks some features. Which ones?

points: Session state does not survive: SET, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY
A connection is shared between clients after every transaction
Older setups also broke named prepared statements
Use session mode, or keep that work in single transactions

cards.title: Zero-Downtime Rename
cards.question: Rename a column on a busy production table without downtime.
points: Expand: add the new column and write to both old and new
Backfill the new column in small batches
Switch reads to the new column, then stop writing the old one
Contract: drop the old column in a later deploy
Each step is its own deploy, so you can roll back
cards.weakness: Which migrations take locks that can take a table down?

points: Changing a column type rewrites the whole table under a heavy lock
CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes
Adding a foreign key or check validates every row; add it NOT VALID, validate later
Any DDL waits behind long queries and blocks everyone queued after it: set lock_timeout

cards.title: 2 Billion Rows
cards.question: An events table has 2 billion rows and keeps growing. Should you partition it, and how?
points: Range-partition by time (one partition per month) if queries filter by time
Queries touching recent data skip old partitions (partition pruning)
Dropping old data becomes dropping a partition, not a huge DELETE
The partition key must appear in queries, or every partition is scanned
cards.weakness: Partitioning vs sharding: what is the difference?

points: Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database server
Sharding splits data across several servers
Partitioning helps maintenance and pruning; sharding scales writes and storage
Sharding adds cross-shard queries and transactions: much more complexity

cards.title: The Vanishing Edit
cards.question: A user updates their profile, refreshes, and sees the old data. Then it fixes itself. What is happening?
points: Classic sign of a read hitting a lagging replica
Or a cache that was not invalidated after the write
Check: does the read path use a replica or cache? What is the lag?
Fix: read-your-own-writes from the primary, or invalidate the cache on write
cards.weakness: Cache-aside: what are the steps, and where do bugs creep in?

points: Read: check the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache
Write: update the database, then delete (not update) the cache key
Race: a slow reader can refill the cache with old data after the delete
TTLs cap how long stale data can live

cards.title: The Hot Row
cards.question: One counter row (page views) is updated 1,000 times a second and everything slows down. Why, and what do you do?
points: Every update locks the same row, so writes queue behind each other
Each update also creates a new row version that VACUUM must clean
Batch: count in Redis or memory and flush every few seconds
Or split into N counter rows and SUM them on read
cards.weakness: Why does splitting one counter into many rows help?

points: Writes pick a random slot, so they lock different rows
Contention drops by roughly the number of slots
Reads sum the slots, which is cheap for a handful of rows
ex.answer:
UPDATE counters
SET n = n + 1
WHERE page = $1
  AND slot = floor(random() * 16);

cards.title: Postgres vs MongoDB
cards.question: Postgres vs MongoDB: how do you choose?
points: Postgres: schemas, joins, constraints, ACID transactions
MongoDB: flexible documents, nested data, built-in sharding
Postgres JSONB gives you some document flexibility too
Decide by access patterns and how much consistency you need
Orders and inventory are relational and need transactions
cards.weakness: When would MongoDB clearly be the better choice?

points: Data is naturally document-shaped and read as a whole (a product with variants, a CMS page)
The schema changes often or differs per record
Write-heavy workloads that need horizontal sharding built in
Few joins: what you read together is stored together

cards.title: N+1 Queries
cards.question: What is the N+1 query problem in Sequelize or Mongoose?
points: 1 query for a list, then 1 more query per item
Caused by ORMs lazy-loading relations
Fix: eager loading (include in Sequelize, populate in Mongoose)
Or a single join, or batching (DataLoader)
Spot it in query logs or APM traces
cards.weakness: How would you spot N+1 queries in production?

points: Query count per request in APM traces (one request, hundreds of queries)
Many near-identical queries in the logs, differing only by id
pg_stat_statements: a tiny query with a huge call count
Fail tests that exceed a query budget per endpoint

cards.title: ORM vs Raw SQL
cards.question: ORM (Sequelize, Mongoose) vs raw SQL?
points: ORM: productivity, models, validation, migrations
ORM hides the queries, which can surprise you on performance
Raw SQL: full control for complex or hot queries
A mix is common: ORM by default, raw SQL for hot paths
Query builders sit in the middle
cards.weakness: What is a migration, and why version it?

points: A migration is a versioned script that changes the schema step by step
Versioned and committed, so every environment ends up with the same schema
Applied in order and recorded in a migrations table
Makes schema changes reviewable and repeatable, instead of hand-edited

cards.title: $lookup
cards.question: What does $lookup do in a MongoDB aggregation?
points: A left outer join to another collection
Adds the matches as an array field (as)
cards.weakness: Why is heavy use of $lookup a warning sign in MongoDB?

points: MongoDB is built around storing together what you read together
Frequent $lookups mean the data is relational and modelled like SQL tables
Joins across shards are expensive and limited
Fix: embed or duplicate the fields you need, or reconsider the database

cards.title: When Not Mongo
cards.question: When is MongoDB the wrong choice?
points: Highly relational data that needs many joins
Core flows that depend on multi-document transactions
Strict constraints: foreign keys, unique rules across records
Heavy ad-hoc reporting and analytics in SQL
cards.weakness: How does MongoDB handle transactions across documents?

points: Single-document writes are always atomic
Multi-document ACID transactions exist since MongoDB 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded)
They need a session, are slower, and have time limits
Good schema design makes most writes single-document

cards.title: include
cards.question: Load orders together with their customer in Sequelize, in one query.
points: include eager-loads an association with a JOIN
Needs the association defined (Order.belongsTo(Customer))
Avoids the N+1 pattern of lazy loading
cards.weakness: What do the four Sequelize association types mean?

points: belongsTo: this model holds the foreign key (Order belongs to Customer)
hasOne: the other model holds the key, one row
hasMany: the other model holds the key, many rows
belongsToMany: many-to-many through a join table

cards.title: MySQL vs Postgres
cards.question: MySQL vs PostgreSQL: how would you choose?
points: Postgres: richer SQL, JSONB, extensions, strict standards
MySQL (InnoDB): simple, fast for straightforward reads, huge hosting ecosystem
Postgres for complex queries and data integrity
Often the team's experience decides; both scale far
cards.weakness: How do MySQL and Postgres differ in storing table data?

points: InnoDB stores rows inside the primary key's index (clustered index)
So primary key lookups are very fast, and secondary indexes point to the key
Postgres stores rows in a heap; every index points to a row location
Postgres updates write new row versions; InnoDB updates in place with undo logs

cards.title: ORM Transactions
cards.question: Create an order and its items in one Sequelize transaction.
points: Managed transaction: commits if the callback resolves, rolls back if it throws
Every query must receive { transaction: t }
cards.weakness: What goes wrong if you forget to pass the transaction to one query?

points: That query runs on a different connection, outside the transaction
It commits even if the rest rolls back, leaving partial data
It can also wait on locks the transaction holds: a self-deadlock
Fix: CLS (continuation-local storage) passes it automatically

cards.title: find()
cards.question: In MongoDB, get the 10 newest paid orders over 100, returning only total and createdAt.
cards.answer:
db.orders
  .find(
    { status: 'paid',
      total: { $gt: 100 } },
    { total: 1, createdAt: 1 },
  )
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .limit(10)
points: First argument filters; operators like $gt, $in, $exists
Second argument is the projection (fields to return)
sort with 1 or -1, then limit
cards.weakness: What index would make this query fast?

points: A compound index following ESR: Equality, Sort, Range
Equality field first (status), then the sort field, then the range field
Check it with explain('executionStats')

cards.title: populate()
cards.question: What does populate() do in Mongoose?
cards.answer:
const order = await Order
  .findById(id)
  .populate('customer', 'name email')
points: Replaces a stored ObjectId reference with the referenced document
The schema field needs a ref to the model
Under the hood it runs a second query, not a join
cards.weakness: Why can populate() on a list cause performance problems?

points: Every populated path is an extra query, and nested paths multiply them
Large lists pull many full documents into memory
Select only the fields you need, and paginate
Or embed the data you always read together

cards.title: Compound Indexes
cards.question: How do you order fields in a MongoDB compound index?
points: ESR rule: Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields
Prefix rule: { a, b, c } also serves queries on a, and on a and b
Each extra index slows every write
Confirm with explain(): look for IXSCAN, not COLLSCAN
cards.weakness: What is a covered query in MongoDB?

points: Every filtered and returned field is in the index
MongoDB answers from the index without reading documents
Exclude _id in the projection unless it is in the index
explain() shows totalDocsExamined: 0

cards.title: Embed or Reference
cards.question: MongoDB: when do you embed a sub-document, and when do you reference it?
points: Embed when data is read together and owned by the parent (order line items)
Reference when it is shared, large, or changes on its own (customers)
Embedding gives one read and atomic single-document writes
Unbounded arrays are a trap: documents max out at 16 MB
cards.weakness: What is the outlier pattern for unbounded arrays?

points: Most documents have few items; a rare few have thousands
Embed up to a limit, then set a flag and spill the rest into overflow documents
Normal reads stay fast; only outliers pay extra
Alternative: the bucket pattern, grouping items into fixed-size documents

cards.title: Pick a Shard Key
cards.question: You must shard the orders collection. How do you choose the shard key?
points: High cardinality, so data spreads over many shards
Even write distribution: avoid a monotonically increasing key alone
Matches the common queries, so they hit one shard, not all
Something like { sellerId, createdAt }, or a hashed key for even writes
cards.weakness: Why is a timestamp alone a bad shard key?

points: Every new document has the latest timestamp
So all inserts land on the one shard holding the top range
That shard becomes a hotspot while the others sit idle
Hash it, or put a high-cardinality field in front of it

cards.title: Aggregation Pipeline
cards.question: Total revenue per seller for paid orders, highest first, in MongoDB.
points: Stages run in order, each feeding the next
Put $match first so it can use an index and shrink the data early
cards.weakness: Why should $match and $sort come as early as possible?

points: Only early stages can use indexes
Filtering first means later stages process fewer documents
Stages have a memory limit; big sorts need allowDiskUse
The optimizer reorders some stages, but do not rely on it

cards.title: REST Design
cards.question: What makes an API RESTful?
points: Resources are nouns in URLs: /orders/42
HTTP methods carry meaning: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
Stateless: each request carries everything needed
Plus pagination, versioning and an OpenAPI spec
cards.weakness: PUT vs PATCH?

points: PUT replaces the whole resource with what you send
PATCH changes only the fields you send
PUT is idempotent; PATCH can be, but is not guaranteed
A PUT with missing fields wipes them

cards.title: Idempotency
cards.question: What is idempotency, and why does it matter for retries?
points: Doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not
Idempotency keys: the client sends a key, the server stores and replays the result
Essential with retries and at-least-once delivery
Upserts on external IDs make syncs idempotent
cards.weakness: Where do you store idempotency keys, and for how long?

points: In a fast shared store (Redis, or a database table with a unique key)
Store the key with the request's result, so repeats get the same response
Keep them at least as long as clients may retry: often 24 hours
Record 'in progress' first so two concurrent duplicates cannot both run

cards.title: OAuth 2.0
cards.question: Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
points: App redirects the user to the auth server with client_id, scopes, redirect_uri and state
User logs in and consents; the auth server redirects back with a code
The backend exchanges the code (plus secret or PKCE verifier) for tokens
Short-lived access token; refresh token to get new ones
OpenID Connect adds an ID token for identity, which is how Google SSO works
cards.weakness: What is PKCE, and what attack does it stop?

points: Proof Key for Code Exchange: the app makes a random secret per login
It sends a hash of it with the login, and the secret itself when exchanging the code
A stolen authorization code is useless without the secret
Required for apps that cannot keep a client secret: mobile apps and SPAs

cards.title: AuthN vs AuthZ
cards.question: Authentication vs authorization?
points: Authentication: who are you? (login, SSO, tokens)
Authorization: what are you allowed to do? (roles, permissions, row-level rules)
OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization; OIDC adds authentication
401 Unauthorized really means not authenticated
403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed
cards.weakness: Is a JWT for authentication or authorization?

points: Mostly authentication: a signed statement of who you are
It can carry authorization data (roles, scopes) as claims
The server still decides what those claims allow
OIDC ID tokens are for identity; OAuth access tokens are for API access

cards.title: Real-Time Options
cards.question: WebSockets vs polling vs Server-Sent Events: when do you use each?
points: Polling: simple, but wasteful and laggy
SSE: one-way server-to-client over plain HTTP, with auto-reconnect
WebSockets: full-duplex over one persistent connection
WebSockets suit chat, live collaboration and games
Scaling WebSockets needs sticky sessions or a pub/sub layer like Redis
cards.weakness: How do you scale WebSockets across several servers?

points: Each connection lives on one server, so servers must share messages
Publish through a pub/sub layer (Redis, NATS) that every server subscribes to
The load balancer must support long-lived connections and upgrades
Plan for reconnects: clients resume and refetch what they missed

cards.title: OpenAPI
cards.question: What is OpenAPI, and how did you use it?
points: A machine-readable spec of a REST API: paths, schemas, auth
Generates docs, client SDKs and server stubs
Specmatic uses it as the source of truth for contract tests
Design-first (spec first) vs code-first (generate from code)
cards.weakness: Design-first or code-first: which do you prefer, and why?

points: Design-first: agree the contract before code; teams build in parallel
Generated mocks and contract tests from day one
Code-first: faster for one team; the spec can drift less if generated
For integrations with other teams, design-first usually wins

cards.title: Rate Limiting
cards.question: Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket rate limiting?
points: Fixed window: simple, but allows bursts at window edges
Sliding window: smoother and fairer
Token bucket: refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to the bucket size
Across many servers, keep the counters in Redis
Reply 429 with a Retry-After header
cards.weakness: How would you rate limit across 5 API servers?

points: Keep the counters in a shared store, usually Redis
Atomic increments (INCR, or a Lua script) so servers do not race
A key per client per window, with an expiry
Or rate limit at the gateway in front of all 5 servers

cards.title: HTTP Methods
cards.question: Which HTTP methods are safe, and which are idempotent?
points: Safe (read-only): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE
Neither: POST (and PATCH is not guaranteed)
Retries are only automatically safe for idempotent methods
cards.weakness: Can a GET request have a body?

points: The spec gives a GET body no meaning
Proxies, caches and some servers drop or reject it
Put parameters in the query string instead
For big search queries, use POST /search

cards.title: Status Codes
cards.question: When do you return 200, 201, 204, 400, 409, 422 and 429?
points: 200 OK with a body; 201 Created (add a Location header); 204 No Content
400 malformed request; 422 well-formed but invalid data
409 conflict with current state (duplicate, version clash)
429 too many requests, with Retry-After
cards.weakness: A user requests an order that belongs to someone else. 403 or 404?

points: 403 says it exists but you may not see it
That leaks information: attackers can probe which ids exist
Many APIs return 404 to hide existence
Pick one rule and apply it consistently

cards.title: Key Headers
cards.question: What are Authorization, Content-Type, Cache-Control and Retry-After for?
cards.answer:
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Retry-After: 30
points: Authorization carries credentials, usually a Bearer token
Content-Type says what format the body is in
Cache-Control says who may cache and for how long; Retry-After says when to retry
cards.weakness: How does an ETag let a client skip downloading unchanged data?

points: The server sends an ETag: a fingerprint of the response
The client sends it back in If-None-Match next time
If nothing changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body
If-Match on writes prevents overwriting someone else's change

cards.title: JWT
cards.question: What is inside a JWT, and is it secret?
points: Three base64url parts: header, payload (claims), signature
Signed, not encrypted: anyone can read the payload
The signature proves the server issued it and nobody changed it
Never put secrets in it; keep expiry short
cards.weakness: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?

points: You cannot change it, so revocation needs state
Short access-token lifetimes plus revocable refresh tokens
A denylist of token ids checked on each request
Or a per-user token version that bumps on logout or password change

cards.title: HTTP/1.1, 2, 3
cards.question: What changed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
points: HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several
HTTP/2: many streams over one connection, header compression
HTTP/3: runs over QUIC (UDP), faster setup, better on lossy networks
Same methods, headers and status codes in all three
cards.weakness: What is head-of-line blocking?

points: One slow or lost item holds up everything queued behind it
HTTP/1.1: a slow response blocks the next on that connection
HTTP/2 fixes it at the HTTP level, but one lost TCP packet still stalls all streams
HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes it at the transport level too

cards.title: Paginating an API
cards.question: Offset or cursor pagination for a public API?
points: Offset (?page=50): simple, lets clients jump, but slow and unstable on changing data
Cursor (?after=abc): fast and stable; no jumping to a page
Cursor suits feeds, syncs and large datasets
Return the next cursor in the response; cap the page size
cards.weakness: How do you design the cursor itself?

points: Encode the last item's sort values (created_at and id)
Base64 it so clients treat it as opaque
Sign or validate it so clients cannot craft arbitrary queries
Changing the sort means changing what the cursor holds

cards.title: API Versioning
cards.question: How do you version a REST API?
points: In the URL (/v2/orders): obvious and easy to route
In a header or media type: cleaner URLs, harder to test
Prefer additive, backwards-compatible changes so versions are rare
Announce deprecations with dates and Sunset headers
cards.weakness: What counts as a breaking change?

points: Removing or renaming a field or endpoint
Changing a type or format, or making an optional field required
Changing error codes or default behavior
Adding optional fields or new endpoints is safe

cards.title: gRPC vs REST
cards.question: gRPC vs REST: when would you choose each?
points: gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, strict contracts, streaming
Fast and typed: good for service-to-service calls
REST/JSON: universal, easy to debug, works in browsers
Public APIs usually REST; internal high-volume calls often gRPC
cards.weakness: Why can't a browser call a gRPC service directly?

points: gRPC needs low-level HTTP/2 features (trailers) that browser APIs do not expose
gRPC-Web adds a proxy layer that translates
Connect protocol works in browsers too
Or put a REST gateway in front

cards.title: HTTP Caching
cards.question: How do Cache-Control directives control caching?
cards.answer:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
Cache-Control: private, no-cache
Cache-Control: no-store
points: public: CDNs may cache it; private: only the user's browser
max-age: fresh for N seconds without asking
no-cache: may store, but must revalidate first; no-store: never store
cards.weakness: How do you invalidate cached data when it changes?

points: Short TTLs so stale data expires quickly
Versioned URLs (app.3f9a.js) for static files: cache forever, change the name
Purge the CDN by key or tag when data changes
ETags for cheap revalidation

cards.title: Webhooks vs Polling
cards.question: Integrating with a marketplace: should you receive webhooks or poll their API?
points: Webhooks: near-real-time and cheap, but can be missed or arrive out of order
Polling: simple and reliable, but laggy and uses rate limit
Best of both: webhooks for speed plus a periodic reconcile poll
Treat webhooks as hints and fetch the latest state
cards.weakness: Webhooks can arrive out of order. How do you handle it?

points: Compare a version or updated_at and ignore older events
Or fetch the current state from the API instead of trusting the payload
Store events and process them in order per resource
Make the handler idempotent

cards.title: Charge Exactly Once
cards.question: The checkout charges a card. How do you make sure retries never charge twice?
points: Client generates an idempotency key per checkout attempt
Server stores the key with status before calling the payment provider
Pass the same key to the provider (Stripe supports it)
Repeats return the stored result instead of charging again
A unique constraint stops two concurrent requests both running
cards.weakness: The payment request times out. What should the client do?

points: The charge may or may not have happened
Retry with the same idempotency key, never a new one
Or query the payment status before trying again
Show the user 'checking payment', not 'failed'

cards.title: Redis
cards.question: What is Redis, and why does BullMQ need it?
points: In-memory key-value store: very fast reads and writes, with optional persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF log)
Rich data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams
BullMQ keeps every job and its state in Redis: lists for waiting jobs, sorted sets for delayed ones
Atomic Lua scripts mean two workers can never grab the same job
cards.weakness: Redis runs commands on a single thread. Why is it still so fast?

points: Everything is in memory, so each command takes microseconds
One thread means no locks or context switches
I/O multiplexing (epoll) serves thousands of clients from that thread
Recent versions add I/O threads for networking; commands stay single-threaded

cards.title: Redis Restarts
cards.question: Redis restarts. What happens to the jobs in your BullMQ queues?
points: Without persistence, everything in memory is gone
AOF with fsync every second loses at most about a second of writes
RDB snapshots lose everything since the last snapshot
BullMQ needs maxmemory-policy noeviction so Redis never drops job keys
Use replicas or a managed Redis for high availability
cards.weakness: Why must maxmemory-policy be noeviction for BullMQ?

points: With eviction on, Redis deletes keys when memory is full
It could delete BullMQ's job data and queue structures
Jobs would then vanish silently, or queues break
noeviction makes writes fail instead, which you can see and alert on

cards.title: Kafka Basics
cards.question: Explain Kafka topics, partitions and consumer groups.
points: A topic is a named log split into partitions
Order is only guaranteed within a partition; the message key picks the partition
In a consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer, which is how you scale
Offsets track each group's position and are committed
Messages are kept for a retention period, so you can replay
cards.weakness: What happens if you add more consumers than partitions?

points: Each partition is read by only one consumer in a group
Extra consumers get no partitions and sit idle
So the partition count caps a group's parallelism
Plan partitions for your peak consumer count

cards.title: Delivery Guarantees
cards.question: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: how does each happen in Kafka?
points: Commit the offset before processing: at-most-once (a crash loses the message)
Commit after processing: at-least-once (a crash causes duplicates)
Exactly-once inside Kafka: idempotent producer plus transactions
End to end, side effects outside Kafka still need idempotent consumers
Most real systems choose at-least-once plus idempotency
cards.weakness: Which did your pipeline use, and how did you handle duplicates?

points: Most pipelines use at-least-once: commit offsets after processing
So duplicates are expected after a crash or rebalance
Make processing idempotent: upsert by order id, or keep a processed-ids table
Be ready to give the real answer for your Fynd pipeline

cards.title: BullMQ
cards.question: How does BullMQ work?
points: A Queue adds jobs; Workers process them
Job states: waiting, active, delayed, completed, failed
Job options: attempts, backoff, priority, delay
Per-worker concurrency and a built-in rate limiter (max jobs per duration)
Workers hold a lock on active jobs; if it lapses, the job is marked stalled and retried
cards.weakness: What is a stalled job, and what causes one?

points: A worker holds a lock on its active job and keeps renewing it
If the lock expires, BullMQ marks the job stalled and retries it
Causes: a crashed worker, or CPU-heavy code blocking the event loop
Blocking code can make two workers process the same job

cards.title: Event-Driven
cards.question: Event-driven architecture vs direct API calls: pros and cons?
points: Producers and consumers are decoupled and scale on their own
Queues absorb traffic spikes
A consumer being down does not block the producer
Costs: eventual consistency and harder debugging
You must handle ordering, duplicates and event schema changes
cards.weakness: How do you debug a request that hops through 4 services and 2 queues?

points: Distributed tracing: propagate a trace id through every hop
Put the trace context in message headers, not just HTTP headers
Log the same correlation id everywhere so logs can be joined
Look at the trace in Jaeger, Tempo or your APM tool

cards.title: The Dual Write
cards.question: You save an order to Postgres, then publish an event to Kafka. The publish fails after the commit. Now what?
points: The dual-write problem: two systems, no shared transaction
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction
A relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka (polling, or CDC such as Debezium)
Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent
Mark or delete outbox rows once published
cards.weakness: Why not publish to Kafka first and then write to the database?

points: If the publish succeeds and the database write fails, consumers see an event for something that never happened
That is worse: phantom orders, wrong stock
The database is the source of truth, so it must commit first
The outbox makes the event part of that same commit

cards.title: Redis Commands
cards.question: What do SET with EX and NX, INCR and EXPIRE do?
cards.answer:
SET session:42 data EX 3600
SET lock:job7 me NX EX 30
INCR views:page1
EXPIRE views:page1 86400
points: EX sets a time-to-live in seconds
NX only sets if the key does not exist
INCR atomically adds one; EXPIRE adds a TTL to an existing key
cards.weakness: How do you build a simple lock with SET NX, and what can go wrong?

points: SET key token NX EX 30: only one client gets it, and it expires if that client dies
Release only if you still own it: compare the token in a Lua script, then DEL
If work outlasts the TTL, two clients can hold it
For correctness-critical locks, add fencing tokens or use the database

cards.title: Producer acks
cards.question: What do acks=0, acks=1 and acks=all mean for a Kafka producer?
points: acks=0: fire and forget; fastest, can lose data
acks=1: the leader wrote it; lost if the leader dies before copying
acks=all: every in-sync replica has it; safest
Pair acks=all with the idempotent producer
cards.weakness: What does min.insync.replicas do?

points: The minimum replicas that must be in sync for an acks=all write to succeed
With replication 3 and min 2, one broker can be down
Below the minimum, producers get errors instead of silent risk
It trades availability for durability

cards.title: queue.add
cards.question: Add a BullMQ job with 3 attempts, exponential backoff and a delay.
cards.answer:
await queue.add('sync', { sellerId }, {
  attempts: 3,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential',
             delay: 1000 },
  delay: 5000,
  removeOnComplete: true,
})
points: attempts and backoff control retries
delay waits before the first run
removeOnComplete stops finished jobs filling Redis
cards.weakness: How do you run a job on a schedule (every hour) in BullMQ?

points: Repeatable jobs: a repeat option with a cron pattern or an interval
Newer versions use job schedulers (upsertJobScheduler)
Give it a stable id so restarts do not add duplicates
ex.answer:
await queue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'hourly-sync',
  { pattern: '0 * * * *' },
)

cards.title: Rebalancing
cards.question: What is a Kafka consumer group rebalance, and why does it hurt?
points: Partitions are reassigned when consumers join, leave or time out
Consumption pauses during the shuffle
Slow processing that misses max.poll.interval.ms triggers it repeatedly
Cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce the pain
cards.weakness: How do you avoid processing messages twice during a rebalance?

points: Commit offsets for finished work before partitions are revoked
Use the partitions-revoked callback to flush and commit
Still make processing idempotent: some duplicates are unavoidable
Keep each poll batch quick so you do not time out

cards.title: Retry Topics
cards.question: How do you retry failed Kafka messages without blocking the partition?
points: Retrying in place blocks every message behind the failing one
Move it to a retry topic with a delay (retry-1m, retry-10m)
After the last retry, send it to a dead-letter topic
Trade-off: per-key ordering is lost for retried messages
cards.weakness: How do you replay messages from a dead-letter topic safely?

points: Fix the root cause first, or they just fail again
Replay in small batches and watch the error rate
Consumers must be idempotent, since some may have half-succeeded
Keep the original key and headers so ordering and tracing survive

cards.title: Out of Order
cards.question: Events for the same order (created, paid, shipped) are processed out of order. Why, and how do you fix it?
points: Kafka only orders messages within one partition
Use the order id as the message key so all its events share a partition
Process each partition sequentially; parallelize across partitions
Retries and retry topics can still reorder: check versions in the consumer
cards.weakness: What happens to ordering when you add partitions to a topic?

points: Keys are mapped by hash modulo the partition count
More partitions means some keys now map to a different partition
Old and new events for that key can be read out of order
Plan partition counts up front, or migrate to a new topic

cards.title: Temporal
cards.question: Explain Temporal in one minute.
points: A durable execution platform: you write workflows as ordinary code
The Temporal server stores every workflow's event history
Your workers run the workflow and activity code
Retries and timeouts are configuration, not hand-written loops
Signals push data into a running workflow; queries read its state
cards.weakness: Signal vs query: what is the difference?

points: Signal: sends data into a running workflow; it can change state
Query: reads a workflow's state; must not change anything
Signals are recorded in history; queries are not
Updates combine both: change state and return a result

cards.title: Monolith or Micro?
cards.question: When would you NOT use microservices?
points: Small team or early product: a monolith ships faster
Every service adds deploys, networking and monitoring overhead
Distributed failures and cross-service consistency are hard
A modular monolith is a good middle ground
Split when parts need independent scaling, deploys or teams
cards.weakness: How do services share data without sharing a database?

points: Each service owns its data and exposes it through an API
Publish events when data changes; others keep their own copy
Accept eventual consistency between services
Shared databases couple services and defeat independent deploys

cards.title: Activity Options
cards.question: Configure a Temporal activity with a timeout and a retry policy.
points: A timeout is required: startToClose or scheduleToClose
Retries are configured, not coded by hand
cards.weakness: Which errors should not be retried?

points: Errors that will fail the same way every time: bad input, 400s, auth failures
Mark them non-retryable so the workflow can handle them
Keep retrying timeouts, 429s and 5xx: they are usually temporary
Retrying a permanent error just wastes time and quota

cards.title: Sagas
cards.question: How do you keep data consistent across services without a distributed transaction?
points: A saga: a sequence of local transactions, one per service
If a step fails, run compensating actions to undo earlier steps
Example: reserve stock, charge card, ship; refund and release if shipping fails
Temporal makes sagas easy to write as plain code
cards.weakness: Choreography vs orchestration?

points: Choreography: services react to each other's events; no central brain
Simple for short flows, hard to follow as they grow
Orchestration: one coordinator tells each service what to do
Easier to see, test and change; Temporal is an orchestrator

cards.title: Circuit Breaker
cards.question: What is a circuit breaker, and why use one?
points: Wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures
After too many failures it stops calling and fails fast
Stops a dying service being hammered and your threads piling up
Pair it with a fallback: cached data or a friendly error
cards.weakness: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?

points: Closed: calls go through; failures are counted
Open: calls fail immediately for a cool-down period
Half-open: a few test calls are let through
Success closes it again; failure reopens it

cards.title: CAP Theorem
cards.question: Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.
points: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance: during a network split, pick C or A
CP: refuse some requests to stay consistent (banking balances)
AP: keep answering, possibly with stale data (social feeds)
Without a partition, you can have both
cards.weakness: What does PACELC add to CAP?

points: If Partition: choose Availability or Consistency
Else (normal operation): choose Latency or Consistency
Even without failures, stronger consistency costs latency
Example: synchronous replication is consistent but slower

cards.title: Notification Service
cards.question: Design a service that sends email, SMS and push notifications for a whole platform.
points: Producers publish notification requests to a queue, not call providers directly
Workers per channel; respect user preferences and quiet hours
Templates, rate limits per user, retries with backoff, dead-letter queue
Provider failover (two SMS providers)
Track delivery status and dedupe by a notification id
cards.weakness: How do you make sure a user never gets the same notification twice?

points: Give each notification a deterministic id (event id + channel)
Record the id before sending; skip if already sent
Pass the id as an idempotency key to providers that support it
Exactly-once is not guaranteed; aim for at-least-once plus dedupe

cards.title: Cache Stampede
cards.question: A popular cache key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. How do you prevent it?
points: Lock: one request rebuilds the value, the rest wait or get stale data
Serve stale while revalidating in the background
Add jitter to TTLs so keys do not expire together
Refresh hot keys before they expire
cards.weakness: What is request coalescing?

points: Identical requests in flight share a single backend call
The first request does the work; the others await the same promise
Cuts load during spikes and cache misses
Many CDNs and proxies do this for you

cards.title: Cascading Failure
cards.question: One slow downstream service ends up taking your whole platform down. How do you stop that happening?
points: Timeouts on every call, shorter than the caller's own
Circuit breakers to fail fast when it is unhealthy
Bulkheads: separate pools so one dependency cannot use every connection
Limit retries (budgets, backoff with jitter) so they do not multiply load
Degrade gracefully: fallbacks and feature flags
cards.weakness: What is a bulkhead?

points: Named after ship compartments that stop one leak sinking the ship
Separate thread pools, connection pools or instances per dependency
A hung dependency exhausts only its own pool
Everything else keeps working

cards.title: Docker
cards.question: Container vs VM, and what is inside a Docker image?
points: Containers share the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and cgroups
Much lighter than VMs, which each run a full OS
An image is a stack of read-only layers built from a Dockerfile
Layers are cached, so instruction order matters
Multi-stage builds keep images small
cards.weakness: Why copy package.json and run npm install before copying the source?

points: Each instruction is a cached layer; a change invalidates it and every layer after
Dependencies change rarely, source code changes constantly
Copying package.json first lets npm install stay cached on code-only changes
Builds go from minutes to seconds
ex.answer:
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

cards.title: Kubernetes
cards.question: What are Pods, Deployments, Services and Ingress in Kubernetes?
points: Pod: the smallest unit, one or more containers
Deployment: keeps N replicas running and does rolling updates
Service: a stable address that load-balances across pods
Ingress: routes HTTP traffic into services
ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration
cards.weakness: Liveness probe vs readiness probe?

points: Liveness: is it stuck? Failing it restarts the container
Readiness: can it take traffic now? Failing it removes the pod from the Service
Startup probe: gives slow starters time before liveness kicks in
Never make liveness depend on the database, or a DB blip restarts everything

cards.title: Helm
cards.question: What does Helm add on top of Kubernetes?
points: A package manager for Kubernetes
Charts are templated manifests
values.yaml files per environment
Releases can be upgraded and rolled back
cards.weakness: How do you keep secrets out of values files?

points: Keep only references in values files, never real secrets
Use an external secret store (Vault, AWS or GCP Secret Manager) with External Secrets Operator
Or encrypt them in the repo (SOPS, Sealed Secrets)
Inject at deploy time from the CI system's secret variables

cards.title: Dockerfile Basics
cards.question: Write a basic Dockerfile for a Node app.
cards.answer:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
points: FROM: base image; WORKDIR: working folder
COPY files in; RUN executes at build time
CMD is the default command when the container starts
cards.weakness: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

points: ENTRYPOINT: the executable that always runs
CMD: default arguments, or the default command if there is no ENTRYPOINT
docker run arguments replace CMD, not ENTRYPOINT
Use the exec (JSON array) form so signals reach your process

cards.title: docker run
cards.question: Run Postgres in Docker, in the background, on port 5432, keeping its data.
cards.answer:
docker run -d --name pg \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:17
points: -d runs it in the background; -p maps host:container ports
-e sets environment variables
-v mounts a named volume so data outlives the container
cards.weakness: Why does data vanish when a container is removed, and how do volumes help?

points: A container's writable layer is deleted with the container
Volumes live outside the container, managed by Docker
Bind mounts map a host folder instead: handy for local dev
In Kubernetes the same idea is a PersistentVolume

cards.title: kubectl
cards.question: The kubectl commands you use most, and what each does.
cards.answer:
kubectl get pods -n shop
kubectl describe pod api-7f9c
kubectl logs api-7f9c --previous
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api
kubectl exec -it api-7f9c -- sh
points: get lists resources; describe shows details and events
logs --previous shows the last crashed container's logs
rollout undo rolls a Deployment back
cards.weakness: kubectl apply vs kubectl create?

points: create makes a new resource and fails if it already exists
apply creates or updates to match the file (declarative)
apply tracks what you set, so later changes merge cleanly
Use apply (or Helm) in pipelines

cards.title: Requests & Limits
cards.question: What are resource requests and limits in Kubernetes?
points: Requests: what the scheduler reserves to place the pod
Limits: the most it may use
Many teams set a memory limit but no CPU limit, to avoid throttling
cards.weakness: What happens when a container goes over its memory limit?

points: The kernel kills it: OOMKilled, exit code 137
Kubernetes restarts it, and it may end up in CrashLoopBackOff
Going over a CPU limit only throttles; it does not kill
Watch for it in kubectl describe pod and your alerts

cards.title: Multi-Stage Builds
cards.question: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile that builds a TypeScript app but ships only the output.
cards.answer:
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
points: Build tools stay in the first stage; only output is copied out
cards.weakness: How do you make container images smaller and safer?

points: Slim or distroless base images
Multi-stage builds; skip dev dependencies
A .dockerignore so node_modules and .git stay out
Run as a non-root user, and scan images in CI

cards.title: Service Types
cards.question: ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs Ingress?
points: ClusterIP: an internal address, reachable only inside the cluster
NodePort: a port on every node; rarely used directly
LoadBalancer: asks the cloud for an external load balancer
Ingress: HTTP routing by host and path to many Services behind one entry
cards.weakness: How does a Service know which pods to send traffic to?

points: Its selector matches pod labels
Kubernetes keeps a list of matching, ready pods (EndpointSlices)
kube-proxy routes the Service IP to those pods
A typo in labels means a Service with zero endpoints

cards.title: Rolling Updates
cards.question: How does a Kubernetes rolling update work?
cards.answer:
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0
points: New pods start, old pods stop, a few at a time
maxSurge: extra pods allowed; maxUnavailable: pods allowed to be down
Readiness probes gate each step
cards.weakness: Blue-green vs canary deployments?

points: Blue-green: run the new version alongside, then switch all traffic at once
Instant rollback, but double the resources while both run
Canary: send a small slice of traffic to the new version first
Watch metrics, then widen; catches problems with fewer users affected

cards.title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
cards.question: ConfigMaps vs Secrets in Kubernetes, and how pods use them?
points: ConfigMaps hold plain configuration; Secrets hold sensitive values
Pods read them as environment variables or mounted files
Mounted files update live; environment variables need a restart
RBAC should restrict who can read Secrets
cards.weakness: Are Kubernetes Secrets actually secret?

points: By default they are only base64-encoded, not encrypted
Anyone with read access to them can decode them
Enable encryption at rest for etcd
Better: sync from an external secret manager

cards.title: Autoscaling
cards.question: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide how many pods to run?
points: It watches a metric (CPU, memory, or custom) against a target
Adds pods when above target, removes them when below
Needs resource requests set, since targets are a percentage of them
Min and max replicas keep it within bounds
cards.weakness: Why can CPU-based autoscaling fail for a queue worker?

points: Workers waiting on I/O (APIs, databases) use little CPU even when far behind
The queue grows but the CPU target never triggers
Scale on queue depth or job age instead
KEDA scales Kubernetes workloads on queue metrics

cards.title: localhost in Docker
cards.question: Your app in a container can't reach Postgres at localhost:5432, but it works outside Docker. Why?
points: Inside a container, localhost is the container itself
With Docker Compose, use the service name as the host (db:5432)
To reach the host machine, use host.docker.internal
Containers on the same network find each other by name
cards.weakness: What does Docker Compose give you over plain docker run?

points: All services, networks and volumes defined in one file
A shared network where services find each other by name
One command to start or stop the whole stack
depends_on and healthchecks to order startup

cards.title: CrashLoopBackOff
cards.question: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff after a deploy. Walk me through debugging it.
points: kubectl describe pod: exit code, OOMKilled, failing probes, events
kubectl logs --previous: the crashed container's last output
Common causes: missing env var or secret, bad config, wrong command, out of memory
Liveness probe too aggressive for a slow start
Roll back first if users are affected, then fix
cards.weakness: What are init containers for?

points: Containers that run to completion before the app containers start
Wait for a dependency, run migrations, fetch config or certificates
They run in order; if one fails, the pod restarts it
Keeps setup tools out of the main image

cards.title: No Dropped Requests
cards.question: Every deploy causes a burst of 502 errors. How do you get truly zero-downtime deploys?
points: Readiness probes so new pods only get traffic when actually ready
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests
A short preStop sleep so the load balancer removes the pod first
terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough to drain
maxUnavailable: 0 so capacity never drops
cards.weakness: What should your app do when it receives SIGTERM?

points: Stop taking new requests (close the server, fail readiness)
Let in-flight requests and jobs finish, with a deadline
Close database pools and queue connections cleanly
Then exit; Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after the grace period

cards.title: Harden the Container
cards.question: How would you harden your containers and cluster for production?
points: Minimal base images, scanned in CI; rebuild for patches
Run as non-root with a read-only filesystem; drop Linux capabilities
No secrets in images; use a secret manager
Network policies so pods only talk to what they need
Pin image digests and sign images
cards.weakness: Why run containers as a non-root user?

points: Root inside a container can be root-like on the host if it escapes
Limits the damage from a compromised app
Blocks writing to system paths and binding low ports
Set USER in the Dockerfile and runAsNonRoot in Kubernetes

cards.title: A Can't Reach B
cards.question: Service A can't reach service B inside the cluster. How do you debug it?
points: From a pod in A: does DNS resolve B? (nslookup b.namespace.svc)
Does the Service have endpoints? Check selectors and labels
Are B's pods ready, and is the targetPort right?
Network policies may block the traffic
Test with curl from a debug pod, step by step
cards.weakness: How does DNS work inside Kubernetes?

points: CoreDNS gives every Service a name: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local
Pods in the same namespace can use the short name
The name resolves to the Service's stable virtual IP
Headless Services resolve to the individual pod IPs instead

cards.title: Terraform
cards.question: How does Terraform work, and what is state?
points: Declarative infrastructure as code
plan shows the diff; apply makes the changes
The state file maps your config to real resources
Teams use remote state with locking
destroy tears it all down, as in FormHook
cards.weakness: What happens if two people run terraform apply at the same time?

points: Without locking, both read the same state and make conflicting changes
State can be corrupted or resources created twice
Remote backends lock the state during a run (S3 lock file, DynamoDB, GCS)
Run applies from CI so only one pipeline touches an environment

cards.title: CI/CD
cards.question: What should a CI/CD pipeline do?
points: On every push or PR: install, lint, test, coverage gate, build
Produce artifacts or container images
Deploy to environments, with approvals for production
Fail fast and cache dependencies
You used Azure DevOps, GitLab CI and Jenkins
cards.weakness: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?

points: Continuous delivery: every change is releasable; a human presses the button
Continuous deployment: every change that passes goes to production automatically
Deployment needs strong tests, monitoring and fast rollback
Most teams start with delivery

cards.title: S3 & EC2
cards.question: What are AWS S3 and EC2, and when do you use each?
points: EC2: virtual servers you manage (OS, patching, scaling)
S3: object storage, very durable and cheap
S3 for files, static assets and backups
Security groups control network access to EC2
IAM roles let EC2 reach S3 without hardcoded keys
cards.weakness: How does an EC2 instance get S3 access without keys in the code?

points: Attach an IAM role to the instance (an instance profile)
The SDK fetches short-lived credentials from the instance metadata service automatically
Credentials rotate on their own; nothing is stored on disk
Use IMDSv2 to protect metadata from SSRF attacks

cards.title: 10x Overnight
cards.question: Your API traffic grows 10x overnight. What breaks first, and what do you do?
points: Find the bottleneck with metrics: CPU, DB connections, queue depth
Stateless app servers scale out behind a load balancer
Database: connection pooling, indexes, read replicas, caching in Redis
Queues absorb spikes; rate limits and backpressure protect the core
Third-party API limits do not scale with you
cards.weakness: Why is the database usually the hardest part to scale?

points: It holds state, so you cannot just add identical copies like app servers
Writes must stay consistent, which usually means one primary
Read replicas help reads only, and add lag
Sharding helps writes but makes queries and transactions much harder

cards.title: Terraform CLI
cards.question: Walk through the Terraform commands from a fresh checkout to teardown.
cards.answer:
terraform init      # providers, backend
terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tf.plan
terraform apply tf.plan
terraform destroy
points: init downloads providers and connects the state backend
plan shows the diff; apply the saved plan to apply exactly that
destroy removes everything in the state
cards.weakness: What is terraform import for?

points: Brings a resource that already exists into Terraform's state
Needed when something was created by hand or by another tool
You still write the matching configuration
Newer versions support import blocks, reviewed in plan

cards.title: Config & Secrets
cards.question: How should an app get its configuration in different environments?
points: From the environment, not from code (the twelve-factor app)
The same image runs in dev, staging and prod with different config
Validate config at startup and fail fast if something is missing
Never commit secrets to the repo
cards.weakness: Where should secrets live in production?

points: A secret manager: AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault
Access through IAM, with an audit log
Injected at runtime, rotated without redeploying code
Not in images, repos, or logs

cards.title: Presigned URLs
cards.question: How can a browser upload a file straight to S3 without your AWS keys?
points: Your API creates a presigned URL: a time-limited, signed permission
The browser PUTs the file directly to that URL
Limit it: short expiry, one key, content type, max size
The API then records or processes the upload
cards.weakness: Why upload straight to S3 instead of through your API?

points: Large files would tie up API servers and their memory
S3 handles scale, retries and multipart uploads
Less bandwidth through your own servers
Your API only signs, which is cheap

cards.title: IAM Basics
cards.question: IAM users, roles and policies: what is each one?
points: Users: long-term identities for people (prefer SSO instead)
Roles: identities that services and people assume for temporary credentials
Policies: JSON documents allowing or denying actions on resources
Least privilege: grant only what is needed
cards.weakness: What is a role's trust policy?

points: It says who may assume the role
For example, the EC2 service, another AWS account, or a GitHub Actions identity
The permissions policy says what the role can do
Both must allow it, or assuming the role fails

cards.title: GCP Map
cards.question: Name the Google Cloud services for VMs, Kubernetes, containers, storage and messaging.
points: Compute Engine: VMs (like EC2)
GKE: managed Kubernetes; Cloud Run: run containers without servers
Cloud Storage: objects (like S3); Cloud SQL: managed Postgres and MySQL
Pub/Sub: messaging; BigQuery: analytics warehouse
cards.weakness: Cloud Run or GKE: how do you choose?

points: Cloud Run: stateless HTTP containers, scales to zero, almost no ops
GKE: full Kubernetes for many services, custom networking, long-running workers
Start on Cloud Run; move to GKE when you need its control
Cost: Cloud Run per request; GKE per node

cards.title: Modules & Envs
cards.question: How do you structure Terraform for dev, staging and production?
points: Reusable modules with inputs (variables) and outputs
A separate root folder and state per environment, calling the same modules
Environment differences live in variables (sizes, counts)
Promote changes dev to staging to prod through CI
cards.weakness: Workspaces or separate folders per environment?

points: Workspaces: one config, several states; easy, but environments look identical
It is easy to apply to the wrong workspace by mistake
Separate folders: explicit, can differ, separate access per environment
Most teams use folders (or Terragrunt) for real environments

cards.title: Drift
cards.question: Someone changed a resource by hand in the console. What happens on the next terraform apply?
points: plan detects the difference between real infrastructure and the config
apply changes it back to match the code, undoing the manual fix
If the change was needed, put it in code first
Run scheduled plans to catch drift early
cards.weakness: How do you stop people changing infrastructure by hand?

points: Give people read-only console access in production
Only the CI pipeline's role can change infrastructure
Keep a break-glass role for emergencies, with alerts and audit logs
Detect drift on a schedule and alert

cards.title: Pipeline YAML
cards.question: Sketch a GitLab CI pipeline with test, build and deploy stages.
cards.answer:
stages: [test, build, deploy]

test:
  stage: test
  script: [npm ci, npm test]

build:
  stage: build
  script: [docker build -t app .]

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  script: [./deploy.sh]
  when: manual
  only: [main]
points: Stages run in order; jobs inside a stage run in parallel
cards.weakness: How do you speed up a slow CI pipeline?

points: Cache dependencies and Docker layers between runs
Run independent jobs in parallel; split tests across runners
Only run what changed (path rules, affected tests)
Fail fast: lint and unit tests before slow integration tests

cards.title: Load Balancers
cards.question: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 load balancers?
points: L4 (network): routes TCP/UDP by IP and port; very fast, no HTTP awareness
L7 (application): understands HTTP; routes by host, path, headers
L7 can terminate TLS, add headers, and do smarter health checks
AWS: NLB is L4, ALB is L7
cards.weakness: How do sticky sessions work, and why avoid them?

points: The balancer sends a user's requests to the same server, often via a cookie
Needed when servers keep session state in memory
They break even load balancing and lose sessions when a server dies
Better: stateless servers with sessions in Redis or tokens

cards.title: What Happens on Enter
cards.question: What happens between typing a URL and seeing the page?
points: DNS resolves the name to an IP (cache, resolver, authoritative servers)
TCP connection, then the TLS handshake
HTTP request, through CDN and load balancer to a server
The browser parses HTML, fetches CSS and JS, then renders
cards.weakness: What does the TLS handshake establish?

points: The server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted CA
Both sides agree on a cipher and derive shared session keys
After that, traffic is encrypted and tamper-proof
TLS 1.3 does it in one round trip

cards.title: Serverless or Not
cards.question: Lambda or Cloud Run vs a long-running container service: how do you choose?
points: Serverless: no servers to manage, scales to zero, pay per use
Good for spiky or low traffic, events and glue code
Limits: time per request, cold starts, harder local testing
Steady high traffic is often cheaper on containers
cards.weakness: What is a cold start, and how do you reduce it?

points: A new instance must boot before handling the first request
Adds latency, from tens of milliseconds to seconds
Keep the package small and do less work at startup
Keep a minimum number of warm instances (provisioned concurrency, min instances)

cards.title: PR to Production
cards.question: Design a CI/CD pipeline from pull request to production, including rollback.
points: On PR: lint, unit tests, contract tests, build, security scan
On merge: build one immutable image, tagged with the commit
Deploy that same image to staging, run smoke and integration tests
Promote to production with a canary and automatic metric checks
Rollback: redeploy the previous image tag; database changes must be backwards-compatible
cards.weakness: How do feature flags change the way you deploy?

points: Deploy code switched off, then release by flipping a flag
Separates deploying from releasing
Roll out to a percentage of users, or turn off instantly without a deploy
Clean up old flags, or they become debt

cards.title: The Bill Doubled
cards.question: This month's cloud bill doubled. How do you find out why and bring it down?
points: Break the bill down by service, tag and project (Cost Explorer, billing export)
Usual culprits: idle or oversized instances, forgotten resources, data transfer, logs
Right-size from real usage; autoscale and scale down at night
Commitments (savings plans) for steady load, spot for flexible work
Tag everything and set budget alerts so it cannot surprise you again
cards.weakness: When is it safe to use spot or preemptible instances?

points: They are much cheaper but can be reclaimed with about 2 minutes' notice (30 seconds on GCP)
Safe for stateless, retryable work: batch jobs, CI runners, queue workers
Mix with on-demand nodes so a reclaim does not take everything down
Not for databases or single critical instances

cards.title: The Region Is Down
cards.question: Your cloud region goes down. What should your disaster recovery plan look like?
points: Agree targets first: how much data can you lose, and how long can you be down?
Backups copied to another region, and restores actually tested
Infrastructure as code so you can rebuild elsewhere quickly
Warm standby or multi-region for critical services, at a cost
Runbooks and regular drills
cards.weakness: RPO vs RTO?

points: RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you can afford to lose, as time
RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long until you are back up
RPO drives backup and replication frequency
RTO drives standby setup; smaller numbers cost more

cards.title: Rebase vs Merge
cards.question: git rebase vs git merge?
cards.answer:
git switch feature
git rebase main      # replay my commits
# or
git merge main       # merge commit
points: merge joins histories with a merge commit; nothing is rewritten
rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch: linear history
rebase rewrites commit hashes
cards.weakness: Why should you not rebase a branch others are using?

points: Rebasing creates new commits and abandons the old ones
Teammates still have the old commits, so histories diverge
They get duplicate commits and painful conflicts
Rebase your own local work; merge shared branches

cards.title: Undoing in Git
cards.question: What do git stash, reset --soft, reset --hard and revert do?
cards.answer:
git stash          # shelve changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1  # keep changes
git reset --hard HEAD~1  # discard
git revert abc123  # new undo commit
points: stash: put uncommitted work aside
reset --soft moves the branch but keeps your changes staged
reset --hard throws changes away; revert adds a commit that undoes another
cards.weakness: A bad commit is already pushed to main. reset or revert?

points: Revert: it adds a new commit, so shared history stays intact
Reset would rewrite history others already pulled
Reset is fine for local, unpushed commits
Lost something? git reflog can usually recover it

cards.title: Pipes
cards.question: From a log file, find the 5 most common error messages.
cards.answer:
grep ERROR app.log \
  | cut -d' ' -f4- \
  | sort | uniq -c \
  | sort -rn | head -5
points: | sends one command's output to the next
grep filters lines; cut picks columns
sort | uniq -c counts duplicates; sort -rn ranks them
cards.weakness: What does set -euo pipefail do at the top of a script?

points: -e: stop on the first failing command
-u: treat unset variables as errors
-o pipefail: a pipeline fails if any part fails, not just the last
Together they stop scripts silently carrying on after errors

cards.title: git bisect
cards.question: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits. How do you find the commit fast?
cards.answer:
git bisect start
git bisect bad          # current is bad
git bisect good v1.4.0  # last good
# test, then mark good or bad
git bisect reset
points: Binary search through history: about 8 steps for 200 commits
git bisect run ./test.sh automates it
cards.weakness: What is git cherry-pick for?

points: Copies one commit from another branch onto your current branch
Typical use: a hotfix from main onto a release branch
Creates a new commit with a different hash
Overuse makes histories hard to follow; prefer merging when you can

cards.title: Bash Scripting
cards.question: Write a Bash loop that gzips every .log file older than 7 days and reports failures.
cards.answer:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
find /var/log/app -name '*.log' \
  -mtime +7 -print0 |
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  gzip "$f" || echo "failed: $f" >&2
done
points: -print0 and read -d '' handle spaces in file names
Quote variables: "$f", always
cards.weakness: Single quotes vs double quotes in Bash?

points: Single quotes: everything is literal, no expansion
Double quotes: variables and $(commands) expand, but no word splitting
Unquoted variables split on spaces and expand globs
Default to double-quoting every variable
ex.answer:
name='G S'
echo '$name'   # $name
echo "$name"   # G S

cards.title: Contract Testing
cards.question: What is contract testing (Specmatic), and how is it different from integration testing?
points: Checks that both sides agree on the API contract (the OpenAPI spec)
Specmatic generates tests from the spec and can stub the provider
Catches breaking changes without running the whole system
Faster and more focused than end-to-end tests
Consumer-driven vs provider-driven contracts
cards.weakness: If the contract itself is wrong, what will contract tests catch?

points: Nothing: both sides are tested against the same wrong spec, so both pass
Contract tests prove agreement, not correctness
You still need a few end-to-end checks against the real system
Review contract changes like code

cards.title: Test Pyramid
cards.question: What is the testing pyramid?
points: Many fast unit tests at the base
Fewer integration tests in the middle
A few slow end-to-end tests at the top
Balances speed, cost and confidence
For integrations: unit tests for mapping logic, contract tests for APIs
cards.weakness: When do mocks give you false confidence?

points: When the mock behaves differently from the real dependency
The real API changes and your mocks do not, so tests stay green
Over-mocking tests the wiring, not the behavior
Back mocks with contract tests or a few real integration tests

cards.title: 100% Coverage
cards.question: Does 100% test coverage mean the code is bug-free?
points: No: coverage shows code ran, not that behaviour was checked
Edge cases and bad inputs can still be missing
Branch coverage is stricter than line coverage
Mutation testing measures how good the tests are
Focus coverage on risky code
cards.weakness: What is mutation testing?

points: A tool makes small changes (mutants) to your code: flip a > to >=, delete a line
Then runs your tests against each mutant
If tests still pass, that mutant survived: your tests missed it
Measures test quality, not just lines run (Stryker for JavaScript)

cards.title: Jest Basics
cards.question: Write a Jest test for a function that adds VAT to a price.
points: describe groups tests; it (or test) is one case
expect plus a matcher makes the assertion
Wrap code that should throw in a function
cards.weakness: toBe vs toEqual?

points: toBe checks identity with Object.is: same value or same object
toEqual compares structure recursively
Two different objects with the same fields: toEqual passes, toBe fails
toStrictEqual also checks undefined properties and classes

cards.title: jest.fn
cards.question: Check that a callback was called once with the right order id.
cards.answer:
const onSaved = jest.fn()
await saveOrder({ id: '7' }, onSaved)

expect(onSaved).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
expect(onSaved).toHaveBeenCalledWith('7')
points: jest.fn() makes a mock function that records its calls
mockReturnValue and mockResolvedValue set what it returns
Matchers check calls and arguments
cards.weakness: jest.fn vs jest.spyOn?

points: jest.fn creates a brand-new mock function
jest.spyOn wraps an existing method on an object
A spy still calls the real method unless you mock its implementation
Restore spies after each test (mockRestore or restoreMocks)

cards.title: Setup Hooks
cards.question: When do beforeAll, beforeEach, afterEach and afterAll run?
cards.answer:
beforeAll(() => db.connect())
beforeEach(() => db.reset())
afterEach(() => jest.clearAllMocks())
afterAll(() => db.close())
points: beforeAll / afterAll: once per describe block
beforeEach / afterEach: around every single test
Expensive setup in beforeAll; per-test resets in beforeEach
cards.weakness: Why does shared state between tests make them flaky?

points: One test's leftovers change the next test's starting point
